♻ ☆ Ultraviolet completion of Starobinsky inflation
Ignatios Antoniadis, Chrysoula Markou, Dimitri V. Nanopoulos
We construct an $N=1$ supergravity action whose bosonic part contains an arbitrary function of the scalar curvature, the so-called $F(R)$ gravity. As in $R+R^2$ supergravity, it can be described in terms of two chiral superfields of no-scale supergravity: one contains the scalaron which plays the role of the Starobinsky inflaton and the other contains the goldstone fermion of spontaneously broken supersymmetry during the inflation plateau. Its (complex) scalar component acquires a non-tachyonic mass in the presence of the string dilaton and can be set to zero, together with the pseudoscalar partner of the scalaron, so that the scalar potential is reduced to the one of $F(R)$ gravity. In a perturbative expansion in powers of $R$, one obtains a small deformation of the Starobinsky cosmological model that solves the problem of initial conditions within the validity of the effective field theory, below the scale of tower of states predicted by the swampland distance conjecture. We also show that a particular example of an underlying microscopic theory with such properties is provided by a four-dimensional heterotic string model containing the Standard Model of particle physics.
comment: minor typos fixed, small clarifications added, matches published version
♻ ☆ Eccentricity-Modulated Phase Degeneracy and Distinguishability between Dark Matter and Accretion Disk Environmental Effects in EMRIs
Tian-Hao Wu, Shu-Jun Rong
Extreme mass-ratio inspirals (EMRIs) are sensitive probes of weak environmental effects around massive black holes, since such effects can accumulate into observable gravitational-wave phase shifts. In this work, we study the phase degeneracy between dark matter halos and accretion disks in eccentric EMRI waveforms. We model the dark matter (DM) environment with NFW and Beta halo profiles, and describe the disk using a thin $α$-disk model. Their distinguishability is quantified through eccentricity-dependent phase diagnostics and the residual signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) in the LISA band. Our results show that DM-induced dephasing depends only weakly on the initial eccentricity $e_0$, whereas disk-induced dephasing is strongly suppressed as $e_0$ increases. The distinguishability time exhibits a smooth and weakly non-monotonic dependence on the initial eccentricity, while being more strongly controlled by the environmental strength. For the benchmark systems considered here, the DM--disk waveform difference can be detectable by LISA, and $e_0$ can serve as an auxiliary diagnostic in addition to the observation duration.
comment: 31 pages, 6 figures
♻ ☆ Mass-type invariants in the presence of a cosmological constant
Virginia Agostiniani, Stefano Borghini, Lorenzo Mazzieri
In this paper, we introduce a new family of mass-type invariants for time-symmetric initial data in space-times satisfying the Dominant Energy Condition. For positive cosmological constant, these invariants, unlike the total Hawking mass, turn out to be genuinely effective in providing new characterizations of the de Sitter solution. From a theoretical standpoint, this opens a new perspective on how one might refine the rigidity statement originally proposed by Min-Oo in his well known conjecture, later refuted by the counterexamples of Brendle, Marques, and Neves. Via a formal limiting procedure, we also define another invariant, the 1-harmonic Mass, for which we independently prove a positive mass theorem and a Penrose-type inequality, thereby extending tools for probing space-time geometries in the presence of a positive cosmological constant.
comment: Minor modifications w.r.t. the previous version: a more detailed proof of the small-sphere-limit Theorem 3.8 has been inserted and a proof of the existence of the weak IMCF with outer obstacle starting from a pole has been added in the new Appendix C
♻ ☆ Probing non-Gaussianity during reheating with SIGW in the LISA band
Gabriele Perna, Guillem Domènech
We analyse the effects of a non-standard evolution of the Universe during the reheating epoch on the spectrum of scalar-induced gravitational waves (SIGWs) accounting for the presence of primordial non-Gaussianity. We show that given values of $w$ and $c_s^2$ leave characteristic features in the spectrum which can be detectable by third generation interferometers like LISA. In addition, we argue that the specific reheating dynamics can suppress or even enhance the spectrum, with crucial consequences for its detectability. We perform a Fisher forecast for different values of $w$ and different scans to assess the detectability of the signal when different values of the amplitude and central frequency are considered.
comment: 21 pages, 6 figures + Appendix
♻ ☆ Redundant Records of the Past: Unifying Quantum Darwinism and Decoherent Histories
Philipp Strasberg
There exist two different paradigms for records in isolated quantum systems: decoherent histories (which determines which past events leave formal records) and quantum Darwinism (which determines which current events get redundantly recorded). Neither one implies the other, and connections between the two are scarcely investigated. We unify quantum Darwinism and decoherent histories based on the insight that only redundant records about past events matter. The resulting framework of past redundancy encompasses quantum Darwinism when applied to events at the current time, and it implies the probability sum rule or decoherence of histories. The Bhattacharyya coefficient (or fidelity) plays an important role to establish this connection. Importantly, various examples show that past redundancy is a more widespread phenomenon than the fine-tuned models necessary for quantum Darwinism suggest. We thus arrive at a richer picture in which redundancy can be caused by mechanisms different from quantum Darwinism (such as macroevents or cascade structures), which emphasizes that redundancy is necessary but not sufficient for objectivity, and which, overall, allows to realistically investigate the question: how generic is redundancy in nature?
comment: Improved clarity and a new result (redundancy implies classicality). One more page. Comments from v1 still apply
♻ ☆ Ricci-flat Seeds, Trombone Rescaling and Magnetizing Kerr Black Holes
Liang Ma, H. Lu
We present a new family of Ricci-flat rotating metrics, which we refer to as Solution II, obtained by demagnetizing the genuine Kerr-Bertotti-Robinson (G-KBR) black hole. Together with Solution I, which was previously obtained by demagnetizing the Kerr-Bertotti-Robinson (KBR) black hole, this gives two families of Ricci-flat deformations of the Kerr black hole, each labeled by $B$. We study the global structures, thermodynamics, various limits, and the local connections among these limits. We also study the remagnetizations in both Einstein-Maxwell and Kaluza-Klein theories, and find that, to yield a physically acceptable solution, the Ernst transformation should be augmented by an appropriate trombone rescaling.

♻ ☆ Regular magnetic black holes with anti-de Sitter cores in scalar-tensor gravity: axial stability and radial instability
Rustam Ibadov, Najibullokhon Shukurullokhon
We construct static, asymptotically flat regular black holes in Einstein-frame scalar--tensor gravity, sourced by a canonical scalar coupled to magnetic nonlinear electrodynamics. Prescribing the density and scalar profiles, we reconstruct the metric, the scalar--photon coupling and the potential. Regularity requires the mass function to vanish at the centre, which fixes the ADM mass, and the central $r^2$ growth of the density to be compensated by the gradient energy of the scalar. The solutions have an anti-de Sitter core supported by a negative potential and a nearly Reissner--Nordström exterior; absence of ghosts restricts the magnetic charge to an interval that shrinks to zero at a finite core depth. Axial perturbations reduce to a symmetric two-channel master system whose positive-definite potential guarantees mode stability; spectral and time-domain quasinormal frequencies agree. Radial perturbations, by contrast, are unstable: the reconstructed potential behaves as $V\propto-\varphi^5$ near the asymptotic vacuum, the scalar becomes tachyonic outside the horizon, and every ghost-free black hole has a growing monopole mode with $ΓM\approx0.14$--$0.28$. An angular Laplacian instability develops near the centre; for black holes it may lie entirely within the inner horizon, while horizonless solutions leave it uncovered and are therefore excluded.

The authors present concepts and mathematical developments which give rise to the Hamiltonian formulation of Einstein's general relativity, first introduced by Arnowitt, Deser, and Misner. All the geometrical quantities needed for the construction are explicitly obtained, and examples of some of the application of the formalism are given.

♻ ☆ Simultaneous determination of Hubble constant and cosmic baryon density: Forecasts for the synergy between FRBs and emerging probes
Peng-Ju Wu, Bo-Yang Zhang, Ji-Guo Zhang, Guo-Hong Du, Shang-Jie Jin, Xin Zhang
Two of the most pressing challenges in cosmology are the persistent discrepancy in measurements of the Hubble constant, referred to as the Hubble tension, and the deficit of baryons in the local Universe, known as the missing baryon problem. Fast radio bursts (FRBs) provide a unique probe of both the Hubble constant $H_0$ and the cosmic baryon density $Ω_{\rm b}$. However, constraints from FRBs alone suffer from a severe $H_0$-$Ω_{\rm b}$ degeneracy that prevents them from resolving either problem. We show that this degeneracy can be broken by combining FRBs with other emerging probes whose degeneracy directions differ in the $H_0$-$Ω_{\rm b}$ plane. Specifically, we quantify three multi-messenger approaches: FRBs paired with gravitational wave (GW) standard sirens, strong gravitational lensing (SGL) time delays, and 21 cm intensity mapping (IM) surveys. The combinations FRB+GW, FRB+SGL, and FRB+21 cm IM each deliver simultaneous constraints on $H_0$ and $Ω_{\rm b}$ better than (1%, 1.5%) in the $Λ$CDM model, and when dynamical dark energy is introduced, the constraining precision degrades gracefully as model complexity increases. Furthermore, within a model-independent framework, both FRB+GW and FRB+SGL constrain $H_0$ and $Ω_{\rm b}$ to precisions better than (1.5%, 3%). These precision levels are based on nominal observational expectations and would improve significantly under optimistic observational scenarios.
comment: 16 pages, 3 figures; accepted for publication in Physical Review D
♻ ☆ Group averaging and the geometry of physical quantum states: from normalizable solutions to solvable loop quantum cosmology
Alejandro Corichi
In canonical quantum gravity the physical states solve the constraints but are typically not normalizable in the kinematical Hilbert space. Group averaging constructs them from normalizable kinematical seeds. We describe the geometry of this seed-to-state map in the language of geometric quantum mechanics. When averaging is an orthogonal projection, the admissible kinematical rays form a holomorphic vector bundle over the physical ray space. The embedded exact solutions form its zero section, and its fibers are strictly larger than gauge orbits. Observables descend to the base exactly when the Hessian of the squared constraint vanishes along their flow. For distributional physical states, group averaging on an explicit Sobolev test space yields an affine bundle of representatives. Its sections are embeddings of the physical ray space whose images contain no exact solutions. The test-space inner product singles out one of them, and narrowing the seed profile gives Weyl sequences of approximate solutions. We apply this to solvable loop quantum cosmology. Group averaging reproduces the Klein--Gordon physical inner product on an explicit test space. Because the scalar-field momentum enters the constraint quadratically, the constraint spectrum has an edge near the shell. The canonical section is then mode-dependent and not Kähler isometric, and the canonical seeds of small universes are biased off the shell. The edge also separates the Page--Wootters state from the slice of the Klein--Gordon solution. An ideal clock shows none of these effects. The results separate the canonical structures, namely physical rays, physical geometry and Dirac observables, from those that depend on a choice of seeds, test space or clock.

♻ ☆ Synergy between CSST and future gravitational-wave detectors: Probing primordial black holes by cross-correlating dark sirens with galaxies
Ya-Nan Du, Ji-Yu Song, Jing-Fei Zhang, Xin Zhang
Gravitational-wave (GW) events and galaxies both trace the cosmic matter distribution, but the mergers of astrophysical black holes and primordial black holes (PBHs) are expected to populate different environments and therefore to cluster with different biases. The GW clustering bias is thus a statistical observable that can separate the two populations. We assess how well this can be done by cross-correlating the photometric galaxy survey of the Chinese Space-station Survey Telescope (CSST) with mock GW catalogs from two future detector networks: the third-generation ET2CE network (the Einstein Telescope and two Cosmic Explorer detectors) and the multi-band BDET2CE network, which adds the space-based baseline Decihertz Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory. We find that CSST combined with 10 years of ET2CE observations can reveal a PBH contribution once its fraction in the total merger rate exceeds about $40\%$, while the much sharper sky localization of BDET2CE lowers this threshold to about $20\%$. The improvement comes from recovering the small-scale clustering information that localization errors would otherwise erase. These results show that combining future GW detector networks with CSST galaxy clustering offers a promising and largely independent route to identifying PBHs statistically.

☆ Predicting $B^{(*)}\bar D{}^{(*)}$ states from a reanalysis of lattice QCD data
Pan-Pan Shi, Miguel Albaladejo, Meng-Lin Du, Feng-Kun Guo, Victor Montesinos, Juan Nieves
We reanalyze the lattice QCD data for the isoscalar $\bar b\bar c ud$ systems with $J^P=0^+$ and $1^+$ at $m_π\simeq 220$ MeV, incorporating both short- and long-range interactions constrained by heavy-quark spin and chiral symmetries. Using the interaction fitted to the lattice results, we predict a spectrum of isoscalar $B^{(*)}\bar D{}^{(*)}$ molecular states with quantum numbers $J^P=0^+$, $1^+$, and $2^+$. The predicted $J^P=0^+$ and $1^+$ $B\bar D$ and $B^*\bar D$ bound states are consistent with the lattice results. Furthermore, the two resonances reported by the lattice collaboration in the $J^P=0^+$ and $1^+$ $\bar b\bar c ud$ channels can be naturally interpreted as $B^*\bar D{}^*$ and $B\bar D{}^*$ hadronic molecules, respectively. We also predict two previously unreported $B^*\bar D{}^*$ states with $J^P=1^+$ and $2^+$: a bound state and a shallow state whose pole may correspond to either a virtual state or a bound state, respectively. Our results provide a unified interpretation of the lattice spectrum and highlight the interplay between short- and long-range interactions in the dynamics of the $B^{(*)}\bar D{}^{(*)}$ systems.

☆ The Effective Field Theory Origin of the Fuzzy Sphere Method
Mykola Dedushenko
Fuzzy sphere Hamiltonians for (2+1)D conformal field theories are usually written directly on the lowest Landau level. We introduce a framework organizing them as descendants of local ``mother theories'' on $S^2\times\mathbb R$. We start with the example of Ising mother theory built from two charged Dirac fermions coupled to a real mediator $φ$. Integrating out $φ$ and the higher Landau levels produces the fuzzy Hamiltonian, while integrating out the fermions gives a conventional local $φ$ effective field theory flowing to the Ising point. Mild modifications of the same theory reach the Gaussian point (tricritical route) and the Lee-Yang continuation. Exploring the space of mother theories, we next promote $φ$ to a complex field $Φ$ and construct a new example, whose descendant is an easy-plane ferromagnet on the fuzzy sphere. Its spontaneous symmetry breaking phase gives a pseudo-Goldstone relativistic scalar, similar to the model introduced by Y.-C. He, while its critical point is non-relativistic, providing the first example of $z=2$ scaling on the fuzzy sphere. Remarkably, it admits exact one-magnon solutions, and the $z=2$ critical point can be found analytically. We then outline a rich landscape of further applications of our approach.

Michael Mandl, Dénes Sexty, Daniel Unterhuber
We discuss the QCD equation of state at temperatures above the crossover and for high baryon chemical potentials, obtained via the first ever complex Langevin simulations at the physical pion mass. In particular, we present continuum-extrapolated results for the energy, entropy, and enthalpy densities, as well as for the specific heat capacity as a function of baryon chemical potential and temperature.

♻ ☆ Non-stabilizerness and entanglement in $(2+1)$-dimensional SU(2) lattice gauge theory using tensor networks
Raghav G. Jha, Jaber I. Taher, Muhammad Asaduzzaman, Goksu C. Toga, Bojko N. Bakalov, Alexander F. Kemper
We study non-stabilizerness (magic) in the ground state of $(2+1)$-dimensional $\mathrm{SU}(2)$ Hamiltonian lattice gauge theory with matter, formulated in the dressed-site basis in the hardcore-gluon truncation and restricted to the zero baryon-number sector. Using matrix product states, we compute three facets of magic: the second-order stabilizer Rényi entropy (SRE) $M_2$, its non-local component $M_2^{\rm NL}$, estimated by the SRE $M_2(\tildeψ)$ of the computational-basis Schmidt representative $\tildeψ$, and a lower bound in terms of the anti-flatness $F$ of the entanglement spectrum. We also prove a stronger form of the sandwich relation: $-\log_2(1-4F)\le M_2^{\rm NL}\le M_2$; the lower bound rests on a stronger inequality that we obtain for arbitrary Schmidt bases and rank, with an optimal constant. Combined with recent results, this yields the unconditional bracket $\max\{-\log_2(1-4F),\,M_2(\tildeψ)-4\}\le M_2^{\rm NL}\le M_2(\tildeψ)$. We emphasize a structural distinction that makes the non-local quantities the physically preferred diagnostics: whereas the full SRE depends on the (non-unique) encoding of the gauge-invariant local Hilbert space into qubits, the non-local magic, its estimate $M_2(\tildeψ)$, and the anti-flatness are invariant under site-local re-encodings and are therefore intrinsic to the state and bipartition. By varying the gauge coupling for two values of the fermion mass on lattices up to $8\times 8$ ($\sim 288$ qubits) with bond dimension up to $128$, we find that the non-local magic, as estimated by $M_2(\tildeψ)$, furnishes a sharper and more bond-dimension-friendly probe of the gauge-matter delocalization crossover compared to the full SRE or the gauge-invariant entanglement entropy, retaining a clear signal at bond dimensions well below those needed to converge the ground state itself.

♻ ☆ Electromagnetic form factors of singly charmed baryons $Σ_c$ and $Λ_c$ in a covariant quark-diquark model
Ye Cao, Cheng Chen, Dongyan Fu, Ju-Jun Xie
We present a systematic study of the spacelike electromagnetic form factors of the ground-state singly charmed baryons, $Σ_c$ ($Σ_c^{++},Σ_c^+,Σ_c^0$) and $Λ_c^+$, within a covariant quark-diquark model. Based on this framework, we obtain their magnetic moments as well as electric charge and magnetic moment radii. Such observables are important to understand the internal structure and the inner dynamics of these heavy baryon states. Our theoretical calculations are in qualitative agreement with available lattice QCD results of $Σ_c^{++}$ and $Σ_c^0$ baryons. We also discuss the mechanism behind the dependence of the numerical results on the charm quark and light diquark. A key finding is that the electric form factors of the singly charmed baryons fall off much more slowly with momentum transfer $Q^2$ than that of the proton, indicating a more compact electric charge distribution, which is attributed to the heavy charm quark acting as a localized core. More importantly, we observe a striking difference in the magnetic structure: while the magnetic form factors of $Σ_c$ are dominated by the light axial-vector diquark, those of $Λ_c^+$ are unexpectedly governed by the charm quark due to the vanishing contribution of the scalar diquark. This highlights the decisive role of the light-diquark spin configuration in determining the magnetic properties. Finally, using an empirical asymptotic relation connecting the spacelike and timelike regions, we predict the total cross section for $e^+e^-\toΣ_c\barΣ_c$. Our findings can be tested at existing facilities including the BESIII, Belle II and LHCb, as well as the proposed Super Tau-Charm Facility.
♻ ☆ Structure of QC$_2$D ground state fields at nonzero matter densities
Ragib F. Hasan, Matthew Cummins, Waseem Kamleh, Dale Lawlor, Derek Leinweber, Ian van Schalkwyk, Jon-Ivar Skullerud
A quantitative investigation into the modification of ground-state field structures in two-color QCD (QC$_2$D) is presented at finite chemical potential. Using lattice simulations with Wilson gauge and fermion actions, we explore the chromo-electromagnetic field strengths under varying matter densities. To ensure accurate measurements, we develop and calibrate two highly improved topological charge operators and evaluate four gradient flow actions. Our results reveal a finite-volume crossover in the regime of the anticipated phase boundary at $μ= m_π/2$, with both chromoelectric and chromomagnetic field strengths suppressed before recovering and exceeding vacuum values at higher chemical potentials. We find the difference between the squared chromoelectric and chromomagnetic field strengths, $E^2-B^2$, to increase in magnitude monotonically with increasing chemical potential. At $aμ=0.7$, we find an $11\%$ suppression of $E^2$, a relatively small effect. A systematic analysis using sigmoid fits of lattice simulations in the crossover regime is performed to confirm the critical chemical potential obtained from the field structure is in agreement with the phase boundary at $m_π/ 2$. These findings provide new insight into non-Abelian ground-state vacuum field structures and offer a foundation for future studies in real QCD.

2026-10-27
Atomic Physics 8
☆ Mediated Interactions between Fermi Polarons in the Strongly Interacting Regime
Renato Pessoa, S. A. Vitiello, Luis A. Peña Ardila
Mediated interactions between quasiparticles lie at the heart of Landau Fermi-liquid theory, yet their behavior in the strongly correlated regime is not fully understood. Motivated by recent experiments [Nat. Phys. 20, 68--73 (2024)], we investigate mediated interactions between quasiparticles emerging from a Fermi sea---Fermi polarons---using zero-temperature quantum Monte Carlo methods. Our main result is that the Landau interaction between polarons remains repulsive in the strongly interacting regime for any coupling strength in the polaronic branch, in contrast to the downward trend observed experimentally near resonance. Deep in the short-range universal regime, our results are insensitive to the microscopic details of the interaction potential, providing robust evidence for the sign of the ground-state induced interaction. In addition, we determine the real-space interaction between static impurities, recovering a Ruderman-Kittel-Kasuya-Yosida (RKKY)-like behavior at weak coupling and the nonperturbative Born-Oppenheimer result at strong coupling. More broadly, our results establish a microscopic benchmark for how Landau quasiparticle interactions survive beyond the perturbative regime of strongly correlated quantum matter.

☆ Experimental evidence for quantum Brownian motion in electron-metal decoherence
Wayne Cheng-Wei Huang, Zilin Chen, Herman Batelaan
Feynman once remarked that the double-slit experiment has in its heart the only mystery of quantum mechanics. Arguably, the scientific significance of double-slit experiments lies in motional decoherence and the mechanism behind it. Decoherence of motional states underpins our understanding of quantum-to-classical transition. It is also central to the operation of miniaturized quantum electron devices and poses a resolution limit for electron microscopes. In this work, we provide experimental evidence for the critical role of quantum Brownian motion in electron motional decoherence. We demonstrate, for the first time, clear signatures of electron-metal decoherence and its continuous tunability. Our experiment concludes a two-decade long search for experimental realization of the Anglin-Paz-Zurek proposal, establishing electron-microchannel systems as viable open quantum platforms for free-electron quantum optics. The quantitative agreement between experiment and theory further paves the way for testing the Caldeira-Leggett quantum dissipation theory with free electrons.
☆ Controlled Dark-State Energy Storage and Work Extraction in V-Type Quantum Batteries
Chia-Hung Chu, H. H. Jen
The performance of a quantum battery depends not only on its ability to retain stored energy against unwanted discharge but also on the amount of useful work that can be extracted from it. Here, we investigate these complementary aspects in an ensemble of V-type qutrits coupled to a lossy cavity. By applying a finite splitting pulse to the two excited states of each qutrit, cavity-bright excitations are converted into atomic dark states, whose populations remain protected upon restoring degeneracy, even while the light-matter coupling remains active. Simulations with finite-duration pulses reveal a capture window governed by the competition among energy transfer, bright-to-dark conversion, and photon leakage. We further show that if the energy is stored in the fully symmetric atomic subspace, the passive energy is bounded by twice the transition energy for number of atoms $N\geq2$. Consequently, if the stored energy scales extensively with $N$, the ratio of extractable work to stored energy approaches unity in the thermodynamic limit. Comparing different initial preparations at equal mean input energy, we find that coherent-state can yield greater finite-time ergotropy despite capturing less energy, whereas Fock-state favors greater extractable work in the stationary component. Our results demonstrate how controlled dark-state population trapping in an atom-cavity coupled system can protect stored energy while providing a conditional route toward high extractable work.

We investigate the nonequilibrium dynamics of a kinetic slush state realized via facilitated excitations in a two-dimensional dissipative Rydberg atom array. Utilizing kinetic Monte Carlo simulations in the strong dephasing regime, we show that tuning the laser detuning to compensate for nearest-neighbor interactions enables facilitated dynamics, while residual next-nearest-neighbor interactions induce kinetic frustration. This competition gives rise to an emergent slush phase characterized by pronounced dynamical heterogeneity and the coexistence of liquid- and solid-like configurations. By probing its nonequilibrium real-time evolution, we uncover a dynamical crossover from isotropic spreading to one-dimensional constrained growth, which can be continuously tuned by the frustration strength. Within this crossover regime, the slush dynamics generate fractal cluster geometries and generalized Ornstein-Zernike spatial correlations. Finite-size scaling analysis supports the system's proximity to criticality. Our findings establish driven-dissipative Rydberg systems as a highly controllable platform for engineering complex nonequilibrium soft-matter phenomena.

We present a transportable stable laser system based on a 10 cm reference cavity and an all-fiber phase-stabilized distribution network for the $^{171}$Yb clock wavelength. We report the successful deployment of the laser system to the summit of Mount Blue Sky at 4300 m, and for the first time, we report 16-digit laser instability measured outside the lab.

The same generator arises under continuous monitoring of a time-dependent observable and under a time-varying complex absorbing potential. Departures from the ideal Zeno limit are governed, in all three settings, by a single positive leakage operator with a dynamical and a purely geometric contribution. Matching the corresponding generators yields a model-independent generalized Schulman relation for the quantum Zeno dynamics in the three scenarios, and a purely geometric bound on the measurement resources needed to steer a subspace along a prescribed path.

♻ ☆ Quantum theory of photonic vortices and quantum statistics of twisted photons
Li-Ping Yang, Dazhi Xu
The topological charge of a photonic vortex is an essential quantity in singular optics and the critical parameter to characterize the vorticity of twisted light. However, the definition of the photonic topological charge remains elusive. Here we put forth a theoretical formalism to provide a comprehensive treatment of photonic vortices. We introduce quantum operators for the photon current density and helicity current density based on the continuity equations from the paraxial Helmholtz equation. Our formalism allows us to introduce flow velocity and circulation for photonic currents in parallel to their counterparts in superfluids. The quantized circulation of the photonic currents is conserved during propagation and it gives an explicit definition of the photonic topological charge as the winding number of a photonic vortex. In particular, we predict helicity current generated pure helicity vortices, in which the photon current vanishes. Finally, we show an interesting effect that the quantum statistics of twisted photon pairs are essentially determined by their spin states.

Our construction provides a physically transparent interpretation of the tridiagonal resolvent and extends to arbitrary permutationally symmetric initial states. In the strong- and weak-pumping regimes, we obtain perturbative transient solutions. We also identify exact relaxation eigenvalues and emission observables at balanced pump and decay strengths. Our solution provides a starting point for extending trajectory-based analytical methods to more general driven-dissipative collective systems.

☆ Classical Verification of Quantum Computation Beyond the Polynomial Hierarchy
Atul Mantri
It is not known whether a classical polynomial-time verifier can verify arbitrary polynomial-time quantum computations with an efficient quantum honest prover without computational assumptions. We show that, relative to a classical oracle, such verification is possible for a language beyond the polynomial hierarchy that is decided exactly in quantum polynomial time. The protocol is public-coin, with perfect completeness and soundness error at most 1/4. To our knowledge, no language with such a proof system was previously proved to lie outside AM relative to an oracle. For every unbounded polynomial-time computable function, the oracle can be chosen so that the message count and the oracle query counts of the quantum algorithm, verifier, and honest prover are bounded by this function of the input length. The message count is optimal up to a constant factor, since for a suitable oracle every interactive proof system for the language uses at least a constant fraction of the messages of our protocol on infinitely many lengths, with a constant depending on its verifier. The language is a variant of recursive Fourier sampling in which code tables encode secrets that address data tables. The tables are evaluated recursively, and the oracle stores only the leaves. The quantum algorithm recovers every secret exactly, and the verifier checks the prover's secrets recursively against random code entries. The recursion restricts the input in a correlated way, as the same secret fixes the code bits and chooses the free coordinate, so Håstad's switching lemma does not apply. We prove a switching theorem for these restrictions, which may be of independent interest. For instances of sufficient height, no constant-depth circuit of size $2^{\mathrm{poly}(n)}$ changes its output with probability above $2^{-Ω(n)}$ when the answer of a random instance is flipped by changing a single leaf.

Dynamical quantum simulations are commonly designed to access a particular response function or correlation function. Yet the underlying protocol prepares a family of many-body states that contains information well beyond the observable for which the simulation was originally designed. In this work, we explore the idea of using these states as laboratories for quantum information. As a case study, we consider the local-pulse protocols used to compute Green functions in finite XX and XXX spin chains, and we interpret opposite source rotations as encoding a classical bit into the many-body system. This allows us to follow how the resulting record propagates, how it is encoded across local subsystems, and how readily it can be accessed with different measurements. We also find a clear separation between representation and readout. While fermionic covariance data exactly reconstruct the signed response in the XX chain, simple spin measurements recover a larger fraction of the locally available information in the XXX chain. This reversed ordering persists when we move from finite-pulse discrimination to local source-angle estimation. Going beyond the source record, the same reduced states also allow us to reinterpret results in terms of Bell state recovery and quantum communication rates, as well as providing direct access to the evolving bipartite and genuine multipartite entanglement of the system. Our results show that dynamical quantum simulations developed for response calculations can naturally be used to ask a much broader set of quantum-information questions about the many-body states they already prepare.

☆ Recovering classical gauge geometry from quantum master constraints

Exact normalizable solutions of quantum constraints form a symplectic submanifold of the space of rays, whereas classical first-class constraints define a surface on which the symplectic form is degenerate. We ask how the degenerate directions can be recovered when quantum theory is regarded as fundamental and the constraints are imposed through a single positive master operator. For a nonnegative master function whose zero set is a Morse--Bott critical manifold, the image of the linearized Hamiltonian vector field is the symplectic orthogonal of the zero set, and coisotropy is equivalent to this linearization having square zero. The image is fixed by the zero set, but the theorem identifies it with the response of the master dynamics, which makes it accessible to quantum states. Three realizations follow. The exact quantum physical space is the opposite, rotational case of the same dichotomy. For quadratic masters, the bottom of the spectrum is $(\hbar/2)\Tr_+L$, so first-class zero sets carry no offset of order $\hbar$; within the harmonic approximation this explains the $\hbar$ versus $\hbar^2$ offsets observed in tests of the master-constraint programme. Finally, the second time derivative of the limiting covariance of a semiclassical packet, which can be determined by bounded probes, has the gauge distribution as its image. Two oscillators at fixed total energy give exact master evolution, an exact realization of this covariance shear, and the reduced symplectic limit. For the non-Abelian SL(2,$\R$) model we compute the coherent and Weyl master symbols, prove essential self-adjointness and a finite-time propagation estimate, and derive the spectral bottom $\hbar^2/2$.

The "Rayleigh limit" is not an intrinsic property of light, but a consequence of sub-optimal measurement of collected photons by the imaging instrument. To overcome this limitation, we present Adaptive Information Mining, a framework that achieves super-resolution by using sequentially refined measurements for incoming photons. Our approach employs a reconfigurable imaging system that dynamically reshapes the instrument measurement responses to maximize the Fisher information and guide scene estimation toward the fundamental quantum limit, even in deep sub-Rayleigh regimes. Importantly, we demonstrate that AIM can be extended to fully blind multi-parameter estimation in scenarios involving an unknown number of sources or turbulence-induced wavefront distortions. Every quantum key distribution (QKD) protocol must limit the information available outside the users' laboratories. In device-independent QKD this is essentially the only assumption made on the devices. In a prepare-and-measure setting it cannot be imposed strictly, since the sender's device must emit a signal that depends on her private input. The natural replacement, and a minimal one, is a leakage bound: a bound on how much information about the input leaves the sender's laboratory, through the intended signal or through any side channel. We ask how far this unavoidable requirement can replace a detailed model of the source. We show that this single bound, quantified by the probability of guessing the input from everything the source emits, suffices to prove security against collective attacks. In our analysis, nothing is assumed about the precise form of the emitted states, their dimension, energy or purity, nor about the receiver's measurement device, beyond the standard requirement that it does not leak Bob's data. The standard B92 and BB84 protocols do not certify any key under this minimal leakage bound assumption. But closely related protocols can and, in the ideal limit, achieve one secret bit per key round. For noisy implementations, we compute key rates using semidefinite programming relaxations. Our best protocols tolerate visibilities down to 0.84, corresponding to an 8% quantum bit error rate, compared with the 11% threshold of standard device-dependent BB84.

The framework integrates orbital geometry, free-space optical and fiber channels, quantum memories, entanglement generation, and Bell-state measurements within a common event-driven architecture. Under the same optimal random seed length, we can replace the $\operatorname{poly} D$ dependence in the number of samples by $O(\log^{1-γ} D)$. Under the same scale of sample size, we can remove their $\log\log D$ factor in the length of the random seed. Our underlying strong quantum-proof extractor has output length $n-O_α(a+\log(1/η))$ and seed length at most $(1+α)\log a+(2+α)\log(1/η)+O_α(1)$ for $n$-bit sources with conditional min-entropy $n-a$ and error $η$. By rigorously evaluating the reduced density matrix of the detector, we derive an exact general expression for the detector's decoherence function, $γ(Δt)$, and use it to characterize the dynamical decoherence of a detector in three scenarios: free space, a perfectly reflecting boundary, and a cavity formed by two parallel reflecting boundaries. We find that in free space the detector's coherence decays monotonically with time, indicating that vacuum fluctuations alone inevitably lead to a complete loss of coherence. In the single-boundary case, by contrast, the detector's coherence displays non-monotonic time evolution: $γ(Δt)$ increases with time up to a maximum and then settles to a steady value, indicating that the initial coherence can be partially preserved due to the presence of the boundary. When the detector is placed inside a cavity, its coherence evolution exhibits oscillatory behavior, and a significant fraction of the initial coherence survives. Moreover, for the same detector-boundary distance, more coherence is preserved in the cavity case than in the single-boundary case. These results provide a viable route for engineering quantum coherence via boundary conditions.

In this paper we study the momentum-space entanglement of this state for a five-dimensional scalar on $M_4\times S^1$ with a cubic or quartic self-interaction. When the zero modes couple linearly and without derivatives to pairs of tower modes, $I_n$ falls as $1/m_n$, where $m_n$ is the mass of level $n$. In the cubic theory, this tail is independent of the ultraviolet cutoff, with coefficient $(μR)^2/1024π^3$ for compactification radius $R$, and the mutual information with the whole tower grows logarithmically with the number of levels. In the quartic theory, the tail is masked by states containing additional hard quanta, which make $I_n$ depend on the cutoff. Compared with the corrections the tower makes to low-energy amplitudes, which are dominated by the lightest levels and captured by local operators, the mutual information with the tower is not dominated by any finite set of levels and arises from the time-nonlocal part of the effective action. The local four-dimensional effective theory therefore describes the low-energy observables of the reduced system but not its state. Unbroken supersymmetry cancels the vacuum energy of the compactification but not the mutual information, which at leading order is a sum of squared amplitudes.

Existing and envisaged devices exhibit architectural differences in terms of register layout and connectivity. Hardware platforms and compiler software stacks are mostly developed independently of one another by different research communities. We conclude that co-design is a requirement rather than an option, and this work provides the vocabulary, archetypes, and compilation abstraction it needs.

Using spin-selective donor-bound exciton optical transitions, we initialize the electron spin and directly resolve its spin-relaxation dynamics. We further coherently drive two spin-selective optical transitions and observe high-contrast coherent population trapping, demonstrating the formation of an optically controlled dark state. At higher driving strengths, multiple dark resonances reveal the hyperfine interaction between the electron and the I = 3/2 Cl nucleus. These results establish the first coherent optical control of a single donor electron spin in a II-VI semiconductor and identify isolated optical donors as a promising platform for solid-state optically active qubits.

In general, up to a small parametric shift of the radial quantum number, the analytic formulas for the energy spectrum can be written for arbitrary power-like potential. A comparison of $E_{BS}$ with the energies $E^{(L)}_{BS}$, obtained for the radial potentials modified by the Langer correction for $d=3$, are in good agreement in general: in detail, it was checked for the quartic oscillator $V=r^4$. It is demonstrated that introducing a dimensionless {\it WKB correction} $γ$ into the r.h.s. of the proposed B-S type quantization condition allows us to reproduce the exact energies with $γ$ being very small for positive degrees $m \geq 0$ and sufficiently small for non-positive ones $m < 0$ for all $n_r, \ell$ studied.

♻ ☆ Objectivity, basis ambiguity, and the classical simulability of concordant quantum computation
Bishal Kumar Das, Sourav Manna, Vaibhav Madhok
Concordant quantum computations, in which circuits whose register carries zero quantum discord with respect to every subsystem at every step, contain neither entanglement nor any other form of quantum correlation, yet no efficient classical simulation of them is known beyond restricted gate sets. We argue that the obstruction is not a shortage of correlations but the absence of a uniquely identifiable local product basis, and we develop this \emph{basis ambiguity} on two fronts. Quantitatively, we introduce the Basis Ambiguity Measure $β\in[0,1]$, the normalized dimension of the manifold of admissible diagonalizing bases on a gate support, and prove a sharp equivalence: a concordance-preserving gate that defeats the Local Basis Finder of Cable and Browne exists if and only if $β>0$. Both directions are constructive. Physically, we identify the resource whose absence the obstruction is: \emph{basis objectivity}, a redundant and independently accessible record of the local basis. We show that an environment in spectrum broadcast form, together with the system--environment interaction map, replaces the NP-hard degeneracy test of Eastin by a fixed number of pairwise fragment comparisons per gate, at a cost independent of register size and circuit depth; the two ingredients live on different axes (state and dynamics), and neither alone suffices. We further prove that a theory in which every state has a strictly unique decomposition into perfectly distinguishable pure states has a simplex state space and lacks the continuity content of Hardy's fifth axiom, so that $β$ is a computational witness of that axiom.

The phaseless auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo (ph-AFQMC) method is a stochastic imaginary-time projection method for computing ground-state properties of strongly correlated quantum systems, whose accuracy depends critically on the trial wavefunction. We present a benchmarking study of trial wavefunctions prepared using parameterized quantum circuits, spanning unitary coupled cluster (UCC), Hamiltonian-informed, Jastrow-inspired, and adaptively constructed ansatzes, and evaluate their accuracy, expressibility, and resource requirements within the quantum-computing-enhanced AFQMC (QC-AFQMC) framework. We find that at similar parameter counts, ph-AFQMC largely removes differences between families for weakly and moderately correlated systems: every trial yields a ph-AFQMC energy within chemical accuracy despite trial energy errors spanning nearly three orders of magnitude, whereas ansatz choice becomes consequential as static correlation grows. Our results indicate that trial variational energy is not always a reliable indicator of ph-AFQMC quality, and that adding variational parameters can lower the trial energy while degrading the ph-AFQMC energy. Across our benchmark systems, trial fidelity ranks trials more reliably than variational energy, and for spin-contaminated trials, the singlet-projected fidelity is more reliable than unprojected fidelity. The UCCSD ansatz initialized from unrestricted CCSD amplitudes provides a robust and inexpensive-to-optimize baseline across benchmark systems, with circuit depth as its principal limitation, while adaptive and compact layered ansatzes remain competitive in accuracy under strong correlation with substantially shallower circuits.

This allows us to empirically improve the learnability of various physical quantum states, including ground states of the transverse-field Ising model and mixed-field toric code, often reducing infidelity by orders of magnitude, and generalizes the basis choice given by the well-known Marshall sign rule in frustrated antiferromagnets. Our results provide an intrinsic complexity metric for quantum states with provable connections to their neural-network representability.

Our key observation is that propagating CNOT faults (\emph{hook errors}) create \emph{stabilizer-induced} trapping sets (TSs) that are intrinsic to hypergraph-product (HGP) and lifted-product (LP) constructions. We obtain these decoders by deriving QLDPC decoders from decoders for the parent classical LDPC codes and using them collectively to correct broad families of \emph{stabilizer-induced} TSs. For CNOT faults that manifest primarily as syndrome errors, we show that their effect is equivalent to a data error together with syndrome-bit measurement errors. Consequently, given repeated measurements and a decoding graph that already includes nodes representing syndrome-bit errors, no distinct variable node is needed for each CNOT fault. Using a \emph{phenomenological} Tanner graph with nodes representing only data errors and syndrome-bit errors, simulations on LP codes show a significant improvement in logical error rate relative to BP+OSD. Moreover, the improved error correction relies on low-complexity finite-state iterative decoders, targeted for fast and low-latency FPGA implementation.

We prove Shor's conjecture: an orthogonal measurement maximizes the information obtainable from any two quantum states in finite dimension. We then show that an error constraint can require three outcomes. For a class of full-rank qubit pairs, the best orthogonal basis switches abruptly as the error penalty increases. Near the switch, three outcomes yield more information at the same error than any orthogonal measurement or random mixture of them. The extra outcome distinguishes confidence levels in one guess; every outcome is used.

On the other hand, given a partition of the set of states of a Markov chain, one can study the corresponding aggregated process. We extend the aggregation technique to the level of quantum Markov chains. We provide conditions under which application of these two operations - Szegedy's quantization and aggregation - give the same result. These consist of the strong lumpability of the underlying Markov chain supplemented by nonlinear relations, generalizing Kolmogorov's cycle condition, that account for the coefficients of both the original and the aggregated transition matrices. In particular, we show that the conditions are satisfied in the case of the random walk on graphs equipped with equitable partitions. We present several examples, which include the classical/quantum walks on Platonic solids. We discuss also relation of discrete-time classical/quantum walks on $N$-dimensional hypercube and the Ehrenfests urn model with $N$ particles. We apply our technique for of discrete-time walks on Cayley graphs of free groups. We also compare our results with those obtained using Cantero-Moral-Velazquez uniformization of unitary matrices.

♻ ☆ Tensor-network simulation of quantum phase estimation in the von Neumann measurement formulation with DMRG-prepared initial states

The von Neumann measurement formulation of quantum phase estimation [Phys.\ Rev.\ A \textbf{66}, 032314 (2002); Quantum \textbf{5}, 465 (2021)] estimates energies by coupling the system to a discretized pointer register through $\hat H\otimes\hat p$ and reading out the pointer after an inverse quantum Fourier transform. Building on these works, we develop a tensor-network framework for simulating and benchmarking this protocol when the system is initialized in a matrix product state (MPS) pre-trained with the density matrix renormalization group (DMRG). The system and the pointer are represented as a composite MPS, the coupling $\hat H\otimes\hat p$ as a matrix product operator, and the coupled dynamics is evolved with the time-dependent variational principle. This gives direct access to the time-resolved pointer distribution, the recovered energy, and the entanglement generated between system and pointer. We apply the framework to quantum many-body spin systems and to electronic-structure problems. For the systems studied, the pointer readout yields accurate ground-state energy estimates from DMRG-prepared approximate states, even when their variational energies are not fully converged. These states generally contain contributions from both ground and excited eigenstates, with their spectral weights determining the corresponding contributions to the pointer distribution. More accurate initial states also strongly suppress the entanglement generated between system and pointer. We also provide logical and compiled resource estimates for a Suzuki--Trotter realization of the protocol.

We show that the harmonic content and bandwidth of the generated comb can be controlled through the applied DC and RF flux bias, and that individual output channels can be selectively addressed by tuning the bus operating point. We characterize the resulting nonreciprocal isolation between channels and discuss the associated design trade-offs, including the influence of modulation depth on harmonic-generation efficiency and back-reflection. Master-equation simulations of a four-qubit array driven by the harmonic comb, together with a one-dimensional line model of the directional conversion, quantify the resulting crosstalk and directional asymmetry; all results are simulations, and no experimental demonstration is claimed. ♻ ☆ Ghosts versus Unstable Particles in Quantum Field Theory

We elucidate the physical nature of ghosts above the multi-particle threshold by contrasting them with unstable particles in quantum field theory. We first consider the asymptotic formulation, where ordinary positive-norm one-particle states can be unstable and decay, whereas ghosts survive asymptotically without decaying, yet admit no particle interpretation due to interference with the multi-particle component which masks the negative-norm one-particle state. This distinction originates from two different analytic structures of the dressed propagator, whose complex conjugate poles lie on the first or second Riemann sheet in the ghost or ordinary case, respectively. Ghost resonances are, in principle, phenomenologically distinguishable from ordinary ones, being narrower and exhibiting weaker interference between positive- and negative-energy peaks. We then formulate the quantum field theory in a finite interval of time and, working within a suitable approximation for the dressed propagator, find that finite-time effects amplify differences in the resonant behavior and give rise to new features, such as higher peaks in ghost resonances. Distinct temporal regimes are also identified: for times shorter than the inverse width, an approximate free-particle description is valid; at later times interactions and interference dominate, leading to decay or multi-particle masking. This study supports the absence of freely propagating ghost particles in the asymptotic limit.

In the Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) era, limited qubit availability and hardware noise constrain the practical deployment of quantum machine learning (QML). Two complementary variants are developed: QSVM-RQNN-V1 performs class-conditioned joint quantum encoding of input and centroid segments, whereas QSVM-RQNN-V2 performs recurrent learning over timestep-wise quantum similarity representations. Experimental evaluation on multiple fault diagnosis datasets shows competitive and, in several cases, state-of-the-art performance compared with QSVM, QNN, QCNN, QSVM-QNN, QSVM-QCNN, and RQNN models. The proposed architectures provide favorable performance-efficiency trade-offs, improved recall, and enhanced fault detection on highly imbalanced datasets. These results demonstrate that integrating centroid-based quantum similarity learning with low-qubit recurrent representation learning provides an effective and scalable approach to condition monitoring and fault classification on resource-constrained NISQ devices.

While LQDL exhibits conventional liquid behavior consistent with the Stokes-Einstein (SE) relation, HQDL emerges at lower temperatures and displays anomalous gas-like transport characterized by superdiffusion and ultralow viscosity, accompanied by a breakdown of the SE relation. This counterintuitive emergence of gas-like dynamics upon cooling reflects the dominant role of nuclear quantum fluctuations, in contrast to thermal fluctuations at higher temperatures. Across the LQDL-HQDL boundary, we identify a transport crossover marked by a qualitative change in the velocity autocorrelation function (VAF), a transition in the Prandtl number, and the emergence of transport minima in shear and kinematic viscosities, thermal conductivity, and thermal diffusivity. These minima reflect a crossover from liquid-like to gas-like transport upon cooling in the low-temperature subcritical region, in addition to the universal transport minima observed in the supercritical regime. The transition from oscillatory to monotonic VAF defines a second Frenkel line, distinct from the conventional Frenkel line observed in the supercritical region. LQDL is a heat-transport-dominated dissipative fluid, whereas HQDL is a momentum-dominated inertial fluid. These results demonstrate that nuclear quantum fluctuations alone induce gas-like liquid behavior and provide a unified picture of transport phenomena in distinguishable helium-4 without superfluidity.

Further consequences include local channel approximation, a thermodynamic limit, and efficient hybrid bosonic-qubit simulation. The point is that these applications are now available uniformly in the input state, as for quantum spin systems, but in contrast to closed Bose-Hubbard systems.

♻ ☆ Combinatorial foundations for solvable chaotic local Euclidean quantum circuits in two dimensions
Fredy Yip
We investigate a graph-theoretic problem motivated by questions in quantum computing concerning the propagation of information in quantum circuits. A graph $G$ is said to be a bounded extension of its subgraph $L$ if they share the same vertex set, and the graph distance $d_L(u, v)$ is uniformly bounded for edges $uv\in G$. Given vertices $u, v$ in $G$ and an integer $k$, the geodesic slice $S(u, v, k)$ denotes the subset of vertices $w$ lying on a geodesic in $G$ between $u$ and $v$ with $d_G(u, w) = k$. We say that $G$ has bounded geodesic slices if $|S(u, v, k)|$ is uniformly bounded over all $u, v, k$. We call a graph $L$ geodesically directable if it has a bounded extension $G$ with bounded geodesic slices. Contrary to previous expectations, we prove that $\mathbb{Z}^2$ is geodesically directable. Physically, this provides a setting in which one could devise exactly-solvable chaotic local quantum circuits with non-trivial correlation patterns on 2D Euclidean lattices. In fact, we show that any bounded extension of $\mathbb{Z}^2$ is geodesically directable. This further implies that all two-dimensional regular tilings are geodesically directable.

While uniform motion can be eliminated by a Galilean transformation, relative motion between interacting systems generally cannot. This mechanism produces magnon currents even without conventional driving forces such as temperature gradients or chemical potential differences. We then introduce motion-induced parametric instabilities. When the emergent scale becomes sufficiently large to resonantly create magnon pairs, the perturbative description breaks down, and the magnonic vacuum becomes unstable. This instability occurs above a critical velocity threshold and leads to spontaneous magnon-pair creation. Connections to related phenomena, including quantum friction, Cherenkov emission, and Zel'dovich superradiance, are also highlighted. The concept of an emergent energy scale provides a unifying framework for understanding transport phenomena and instabilities in quantum systems with relative motion.
comment: Accepted for publication in Materials for Quantum Technology
♻ ☆ The Natural Formulation of Cubic-Phase Dynamics in the Linear Potential
Maximilian L. D. D. Pellner, Georgi Gary Rozenman
A quantum wave packet in a linear potential, i.e. a constant force such as gravity, accumulates a cubic-in-time phase, universal across Schrödinger-type platforms. The natural formulation of the cubic phase dynamics follows from their canonical realization, the Airy eigenstates. The eigenforce, the potential gradient for which the Airy profile is stationary and hence the intrinsic force behind its known self-acceleration absent any applied force, derives from the eigenvalue problem and characterizes the state uniquely up to a rigid translation. Alongside the applied force, it underlies the analytically closed form of these dynamics, comprising three known contributions, intrinsic, force-induced, and a cross term. The force-induced one alone is shape-independent, whereas the Airy eigenstate renders the other two non-dispersing. The cubic coefficient factorizes into two Newtonian force balances, vanishing at the stationary eigenstate and at a non-trivial zero where the phase cancels while the packet keeps accelerating. This exposes the eigenforce as an effective antagonist to the applied force, not only in the caustic's self-acceleration but here also within the phase, while leaving the centroid untouched by Ehrenfest's theorem. Spatially uniform within each packet, it escapes direct measurement, accessible only as the relative phase of two colliding packets, each in its own potential. The relative cubic coefficient is symmetry-forbidden for identical packets and activated by preparation asymmetry. Simulated interference of two truncated Airy packets demonstrates the extraction. Spanning ultracold atoms, paraxial optics, and surface-gravity water waves, it provides a platform-independent probe of the cubic phase and, through its force dependence, of the constant force itself.
comment: 9 pages, 4 figures. Revised version. Corrected numerical results, expanded derivation and a new appendix with the simulation parameters. Title changed
♻ ☆ Operator quantum singular value transformation: Spectral mapping, design and topological invariants
Chusei Kiumi, Yohei Tanaka, Akito Suzuki
Quantum singular value transformation (QSVT) provides a unifying framework for quantum algorithms by applying the polynomials of quantum signal processing (QSP) to block-encoded matrices. We connect this framework with spectral analysis, design and topological protection in condensed matter physics. Extending QSVT beyond matrices to possibly infinite-dimensional operators (operator QSVT), we establish the following. First, it transforms every block of the operator by the QSP polynomials; no singular value decomposition is needed. Second, a spectral mapping theorem determines the full spectrum of the QSVT operator, including continuous spectra, from the embedded operator through the QSP polynomial, allowing spectral analysis without translation invariance. Third, the spectral mapping turns QSP into spectral design: the QSP phases can stretch, fold and separate the bands and place the eigenvalues. Finally, the kernel sectors that conventional QSVT usually sets aside carry a topological index, invariant under the choice of QSP phases, local perturbations and gap-preserving deformations, which guarantees topologically protected states. These results unify two quantum walks: Szegedy's walk from quantum algorithms and the split-step walk from condensed matter physics. Their kernel sectors encode the graph's Euler characteristic and the difference of bulk winding numbers, respectively. For the split-step walk, QSP breaks chiral symmetry but not the topological protection, and can move the protected state into a continuous band to form a bound state in the continuum (BIC).
comment: 30 pages, 5 figures
♻ ☆ On the uniqueness of translation-invariant ground states of the $S=1$ Heisenberg and $J$--$D$ antiferromagnetic chains
Hal Tasaki
Using the analytic machinery and numerical inputs of OpenAI's proofs of the Haldane gap, we prove uniqueness of the translation-invariant ground state of the infinite $S=1$ Heisenberg antiferromagnetic chain and of the $J$-$D$ model for sufficiently small $|D|$. Uniqueness is among all translation-invariant ground states in the operator-algebraic sense, without assuming a gap or spin-rotation symmetry for a competing state. The proof combines concentration of the spatial transfer spectrum, an exponentially small low-temperature free-energy correction, and a Golden--Thompson comparison for separated local observables. The unique translation-invariant state is pure, locally unique and gapped, and continuous in $D$. The ground states of even periodic chains and odd open chains with equal positive endpoint fields converge to this state along their full sequences, uniformly in $D$, with a stretched-exponential local rate. Every choice of ground states of open chains without endpoint magnetic fields has the same local limit. These conclusions do not establish uniqueness among arbitrary nontranslation-invariant ground states of the infinite chain. The author formulated the problems and proposed the core strategies. ChatGPT Astra made substantial contributions to developing the proofs and preparing the manuscript.
comment: 46 pages, 2 figures. Version 2: The title has been changed. We prove uniqueness among translation-invariant ground states of the infinite chain, a substantially stronger result than the boundary-condition independence established in version 1
♻ ☆ Discovering quantum phenomena with Interpretable Machine Learning
Paulin de Schoulepnikoff, Hendrik Poulsen Nautrup, Hans J. Briegel, Gorka Muñoz-Gil
Interpretable machine learning techniques are becoming essential tools for extracting physical insights from complex quantum data. We build on recent advances in variational autoencoders to demonstrate that such models can learn physically meaningful and interpretable representations from a broad class of unlabeled quantum datasets. From raw measurement data alone, the learned representation reveals rich information about the underlying structure of quantum phase diagrams. We further augment the learning pipeline with symbolic methods, enabling the discovery of compact analytical descriptors that serve as order parameters for the distinct regimes emerging in the learned representations. We demonstrate the framework on experimental Rydberg-atom snapshots, classical shadows of the cluster Ising model, and hybrid discrete-continuous fermionic data, revealing previously unreported phenomena such as a corner-ordering pattern in the Rydberg arrays. These results establish a general framework, which constitutes an important step toward the autonomous discovery of physical descriptors from diverse quantum datasets. All methods are available through qdisc, an open-source Python library designed to make these tools accessible to the broader community.
♻ ☆ Scalable Quantum Machine Learning: Trainability, Expressivity and Efficiency
Iordanis Kerenidis
Scalable parameterized quantum circuits for machine learning face three obstacles: barren plateaus, no guarantee the learned function class is classically hard, and prohibitive circuit evaluations per gradient step. We propose the unitary brick-wall: a $k$-particle fermionic architecture for nearest-neighbor hardware, combining Reconfigurable Beam Splitters with interleaved single-qubit phases and a non-Gaussian magic-state encoding, where $k$ trades classical hardness against training cost. Trainable. The brick-wall has dynamical Lie algebra $\mathfrak{u}(n)$ and is surjective onto $U(n)$ via Givens rotations, enabling Haar initialization. Two-body correlator readouts achieve gradient variance $Θ(k^3/n^5)$, polynomial in $n$ throughout $n-2k=Ω(n)$. Expressive. Hardness is controlled by $k$: best-known classical sampling runs in time $2^{Θ(k)}$, worst-case #P-hardness holds from $k=n^ε$, and the average-case machinery of Fermion Sampling applies at $k=Θ(n)$. The sampler is input-dependent, so costs are paid per query: at our operating point $k=100$ one query needs $\sim 10^{15}$ operations, beyond commercial query rates, and at $k=120$ an exascale machine sustains under one query per second. Efficient. A multi-layer parallel parameter-shift rule computes all $O(n^2)$ gradients from $4kn$ circuit evaluations per step, a factor $n/k$ reduction over the standard rule's $4n^2$, growing linearly with $n$ at fixed $k$. The unitary butterfly targets all-to-all hardware, with $2\log n$ layers of parallel gates and $(3/2)n\log n$ parameters, similar hardness guarantees, and $4k\log n$ evaluations per step -- the same factor-$n/k$ reduction. Its trainability holds at two levels: absence of exponential barren plateaus is unconditional, while the sharp $Θ(k^3/n^5)$ rate needs a conjectured scalar comparison with the two-particle Haar second moment.

Classical sampling cost and operating point updated to the best currently known algorithm. The two-particle design conjecture is restated as a scalar comparison. No trainability, parameter-shift or hardness conclusion changes
♻ ☆ A Control Line Multiplexing Framework for Scalable Quantum Computing
Dayu Li, Naibin Zhou, Zhiyuan Chen, Zihua Chen, Yu Xu, Yuan Li, Daojin Fan, Wenhao Chu, Xiawei Chen, Hui Deng, Jiacheng Gui, Linyin Hong, Bo Fan, Weiping Lin, Haonan Zou, Haoxin Lou, Xintao Zhao, Sirui Cao, Ying Chong, Qingling Zhu, Chen Wang, Yisen Hu, Kaili Zhang, Feifan Su, Haibin Zhang, Jianghan Yin, Yajie Du, Yinan Jiang, Haoping Luo, Weifeng Yang, Jiafei Wang, Jin Lin, Futian Liang, Hao Rong, Kai Yan, Ming Gong, Jinjin Li, Maliang Liu, Cheng-Zhi Peng, Shaowei Li, Xiaobo Zhu, Jian-Wei Pan
Universal fault-tolerant superconducting quantum computers are expected to require millions of physical qubits; yet extending the prevailing dedicated-control-line paradigm to this scale would exceed the wiring density and cooling-power budget of dilution refrigerators. Microwave frequency-division multiplexing (FDM) revolutionized classical communications by enabling many independent channels to share common transmission infrastructure. Translating this principle to superconducting quantum control, however, requires an all-microwave architecture and experimental validation of frequency-multiplexed gate control. Recent work in quantum error correction has demonstrated microwave-based readout, single-qubit gates and leakage suppression, whereas two-qubit gates remain predominantly driven by unipolar pulses and thus constitute the missing element of an all-microwave architecture. Here, we propose a periodically extensible hybrid multiplexing framework in which all gate operations are frequency-division multiplexed using polychromatic microwave pulses and band-pass filters, thereby reducing the required control-line count by one to two orders of magnitude. In a 1:4 demonstration, we achieve average errors of $(6.4\pm0.2)\times10^{-3}$ for parallel FDM CZ gates and $(10.6\pm0.2)\times10^{-4}$ for parallel FDM $XY(π/2)$ gates, without statistically significant multiplexing-induced degradation. Together with on-chip DC sources, this FDM-based gate-control scheme completes the last missing module in a scalable multiplexed-control architecture toward universal fault-tolerant quantum computing.
comment: 22 pages, 4 figures, 1 table; includes 11 pages of supplementary material with 14 figures and 2 tables
♻ ☆ Utilizing Partitioning for Distributed Tensor Network Contraction
Manuel Geiger, Qunsheng Huang, Christian B. Mendl
Tensor networks have proven to be a valuable tool, for instance, in the classical simulation of (strongly correlated) quantum systems. As the size of the systems increases, contracting larger tensor networks becomes computationally demanding. In this work, we explore the use of partitioning to distribute the contraction task across a distributed memory architecture, commonly found in high-performance computing environments. This approach offers a promising alternative to the widely used parallelization based on slicing, which often incurs significant computational overhead. We particularly investigate how a given partitioning can be optimized to enable efficient contraction, as both computational and memory costs are highly sensitive to the chosen strategy. To this end, we introduce a simulated annealing-based method that iteratively refines a partitioning to minimize the operation count along the critical path, thereby reducing time-to-solution. The algorithm is evaluated on MQT Bench circuits and achieves a lower computational cost in 47 of 71 circuits, with improvements up to 5 orders of magnitude compared to contraction paths generated by Cotengra, a state-of-the-art contraction path finding library.
comment: 22 pages, 10 figures
♻ ☆ Entanglement of momenta at colliders
Marco Fabbrichesi, Roberto Floreanini, Luca Marzola
We investigate the entanglement in the momenta of particle pairs produced at colliders, discarding the information on their spin state. We show how to quantify this entanglement by reducing the continuous momentum variables to a two-qubit system through hemispherical projections. We discuss in detail the production of $τ$-lepton pairs at an electron collider. In the Standard Model, the discretized momenta are in a genuinely maximally entangled pure state for suitable choices of the hemispheres.
comment: 11 pages
♻ ☆ Quantum theory of photonic vortices and quantum statistics of twisted photons
Li-Ping Yang, Dazhi Xu
The topological charge of a photonic vortex is an essential quantity in singular optics and the critical parameter to characterize the vorticity of twisted light. However, the definition of the photonic topological charge remains elusive. Here we put forth a theoretical formalism to provide a comprehensive treatment of photonic vortices. We introduce quantum operators for the photon current density and helicity current density based on the continuity equations from the paraxial Helmholtz equation. Our formalism allows us to introduce flow velocity and circulation for photonic currents in parallel to their counterparts in superfluids. The quantized circulation of the photonic currents is conserved during propagation and it gives an explicit definition of the photonic topological charge as the winding number of a photonic vortex. In particular, we predict helicity current generated pure helicity vortices, in which the photon current vanishes. Finally, we show an interesting effect that the quantum statistics of twisted photon pairs are essentially determined by their spin states.

♻ ☆ Universal Quantum Gate Set for Multi-Mode Schrödinger Cat States Stabilized by Non-Local Dissipation Engineering
Jesper Lind-Olsen, Jonas Lidal, Tron Omland, Joakim Bergli
Schrödinger cat states provide a hardware-efficient platform for bosonic quantum error correction by encoding logical information in protected manifolds of harmonic oscillators. While previous work has demonstrated the dissipative stabilization of multi-mode Schrödinger cat states as robust quantum memories, a framework for universal quantum computation has remained unavailable. Here we work towards this by introducing a universal gate set for dissipatively stabilized multi-mode cat qubits as a necessary resource for computation. Using a chain of Kerr non-linear oscillators coupled through engineered non-local dissipation and an effective low-dimensional description, we show how single-qubit control can be achieved through arbitrary rotation around the $X$-axis and $π/2$-rotation around the $Z$-axis. We further show how coupling two such stabilized arrays through just one oscillator on each respective array enables coherent entangling operations through implementation of the $XX_{π/2}$ gate. Numerical simulations demonstrate high-fidelity gate dynamics and entanglement generation under realistic parameters. Finally, we analyze the effects of induced and intrinsic photon loss, disorder, and the validity regime of the effective low-dimensional theory. Our results establish dissipatively stabilized multi-mode Schrödinger cat states as a potential architecture for universal bosonic quantum computation.

♻ ☆ Quantum structured light: Non-classical spin texture of twisted single-photon pulses
Li-Ping Yang, Zubin Jacob
Classical structured light with controlled polarization and orbital angular momentum (OAM) of electromagnetic waves has varied applications in optical trapping, bio-sensing, optical communications and quantum simulations. The classical electromagnetic theory of such structured light beams and pulses have advanced significantly over the last two decades. However, a framework for the quantum density of spin and OAM for single-photons remains elusive. Here, we develop a theoretical framework and put forth the concept of quantum structured light for space-time wavepackets at the single-photon level. Our work marks a paradigm shift beyond scalar-field theory as well as the paraxial approximation and can be utilized to study the quantum properties of the spin and OAM of all classes of twisted quantum light pulses. We capture the uncertainty in full three-dimensional (3D) projections of vector spin demonstrating their quantum behavior beyond the conventional concept of classical polarization. Even in laser beams with high OAM along the propagation direction, we predict the existence of large OAM quantum fluctuations in the transverse plane which can be verified experimentally. We show that the spin density generates modulated helical texture beyond the paraxial limit and exhibits distinct statistics for Fock-state vs. coherent-state twisted pulses. We introduce the quantum correlator of photon spin density to characterize the nonlocal spin noise providing a rigorous parallel with fermionic spin noise operators. Our work paves the way for quantum spin-OAM physics in twisted single photon pulses and also opens explorations for new phases of light with long-range spin order.
comment: We corrected the observable photon OAM by retaining the polarization-frame connection and revised the resulting OAM mean values, fluctuations, and uncertainty relations. All corrections are highlighted in red
♻ ☆ Maximally Sliced States as a Framework for Quantum Coherence, Entanglement, and Teleportation under Decoherence
Anushree Pandey, Sovik Roy
Quantum resources such as coherence and entanglement need not exhibit the same dependence on the parameters of a quantum state, and their responses to decoherence can differ qualitatively. We investigate these relationships using the three-qubit maximally sliced (MS) state, whose continuous parameter provides a tunable framework for redistributing quantum correlations. We analyze the relative entropy of coherence, (l_1)-norm coherence, and basis-independent coherence of the tripartite MS state and compare their behavior with the three-tangle. We then trace out one qubit and study the coherence, concurrence, and optimal teleportation fidelity of the resulting bipartite state. For this reduced state, the concurrence coincides with the (l_1)-norm coherence because both are determined by the same off-diagonal matrix element. We further examine the effects of amplitude damping and dephasing. Amplitude damping changes both populations and coherence, whereas dephasing preserves populations while suppressing phase coherence. The three coherence measures respond differently to these channels, showing that no single coherence measure fully characterizes decoherence. Under dephasing, the concurrence remains directly related to the (l_1)-norm coherence, yielding the teleportation-fidelity relation (f^T=(2+C)/3). Our results demonstrate that the MS family provides a useful tunable setting for distinguishing basis-dependent and basis-independent coherence and for studying the different responses of entanglement and teleportation resources to dissipative and phase-decoherence processes.
