☆ A no-go theorem for closed timelike curves in globally null-foliated spacetimes
Hongsheng Zhang
The study of closed timelike curves has proceeded one spacetime at a time, and the criteria available form three families, the time function criteria, the energy condition criteria, and the topological criteria. We initiate a fourth family of criteria, elementary in form and resting on a single scalar equation rather than any energy condition. We prove that a spacetime admitting a globally defined function whose gradient is everywhere null cannot contain a closed timelike curve, and that the hypothesis is logically independent of stable causality rather than weaker than it. The proof turns on one algebraic fact, that a null covector is never orthogonal to a timelike vector, so the function grows strictly along every timelike curve and cannot close. Because the null eikonal equation alone decides the criterion, we can use it where the classical time function theorem is silent. We establish for the first time that no Kundt spacetime and no Robinson--Trautman spacetime can contain a closed timelike curve on any region where the null coordinate is globally single valued, whatever the cosmological constant and the rotation one form, which settles a question left open for gyratonic waves. We further show that the Misner, Ori and Ahmed constructions reduce to the statement that a compact null direction has turned timelike, and that the cosmological constant, the expansion and the shear are spectators in all of them.

We also separate stability within the collective-coordinate ansatz from full radial perturbative stability and specify the range in which the non-relativistic treatment is reliable. In pulsar timing array analyses, the stochastic process describing the gravitational wave background is typically modeled using a Fourier basis at discrete frequencies with an interval $\sim 0.1~\mathrm{yr}^{-1}$, with a diagonal Fourier-domain covariance determined by the power spectral density at the corresponding frequencies. Although this rank-reduced modeling significantly accelerates likelihood evaluation and provides a good approximation in many scenarios, it can lead to biased parameter inference because it is insensitive to spectral features on scales smaller than $\sim 0.1~\mathrm{yr}^{-1}$. We introduce a better construction of the low-rank covariance for low-frequency processes by maximizing the log-likelihood averaged over an ensemble of realizations drawn from the true model likelihood. In this approach, the basis-domain covariance matrix is sensitive to the entire model spectrum and is generally non-diagonal. Using two mock datasets, we demonstrate improved likelihood accuracy and more faithful recovery of spectral features compared to the conventional Fourier-diagonal model. Benchmark tests show that this new model requires a computational cost comparable to that of the conventional approach.

For SKA-PTA, we forecast sensitivities down to $m_g \sim 10^{-24}\,\mathrm{eV}/c^{2}$ with a 10-year observing baseline and $m_g \sim 10^{-25}\,\mathrm{eV}/c^{2}$ with a 50-year observing baseline, representing order-of-magnitude improvements over current limits. Quantum information concepts and quantum technologies have opened the prospect of probing the quantum nature of gravity in table-top experiments. Most proposals rely on detecting gravitationally mediated entanglement, which requires measurements on both interacting systems. Here we propose an alternative test based on witnessing quantum memory effects in the dynamics of a single system. We show how the quantum memory concept allows the non-classicality of the interaction between two systems to be certified through local measurements on only one of them. We then develop a novel quantum memory witness, making the approach applicable to gravitationally coupled harmonic oscillators. This witness requires no assumptions about the dynamics, such as Gaussianity. Our results show that the quantumness of gravitational dynamics can be certified with access to only one subsystem, opening the door to asymmetric implementations that can offer conceptual and experimental advantages to probing the quantum nature of the gravitational interaction.

The modified Friedmann equations depend on an entropy exponent $m$, an MHR coupling parameter $γ$, and an entanglement-correction amplitude $f_B$, with standard $Λ$CDM recovered in the appropriate limit. Freeing the MHR coupling parameter or the entanglement amplitude raises the inferred Hubble constant to $h\simeq0.70$-$0.71$, reducing the CMB-SH0ES tension from ${\sim}4σ$ to ${\sim}1.2$-$2.6σ$, but no scenario fully resolves it within a flat universe. ♻ ☆ On the nature of the black hole information problem
Thiago T. Bergamaschi
The aim of this work is to present the black hole information problem and discuss the assumptions and hypotheses necessary for its formulation. As the problem arises in the framework of semiclassical gravity, we first review the necessary notions to describe Lorentzian manifolds equipped with physical properties, as well as the physical concepts of the theory that describes the gravitational interaction as the curvature of spacetime, general relativity. From its classical perspective, we develop the formalism to study the dynamical aspects of black holes in spacetimes obeying suitable causality conditions. Equipped with conjectures that nature censors naked singularities and that black holes reach a stationary configuration after they form, the black hole uniqueness theorems allow us to review several relations for the geometrical quantities associated with them. Following considerations of the other fundamental interactions, which are described by quantum field theory, we review the arguments in the formalism of quantum field theory in curved spacetime that give rise to the effective particle creation effect, its approximately thermal character, and the concept of black hole evaporation. With a precise quantification of information in quantum mechanics and assuming that the condition for physically acceptable states is given by the Hadamard condition, we review the result that entanglement between causally complementary regions is an intrinsic feature of quantum field theory. As a consequence, we discuss how the formation and complete evaporation of black holes leads to information loss. Conscious that such a prediction follows if no deviations from the semiclassical picture occur at the Planck scale, we discuss alternatives to this nonunitary dynamical evolution and formulate the black hole information problem. Lastly, we analyze the assumptions and hypotheses that lead to the problem.

Assessing possible life on an exoplanet requires spatial, spectral, temporal, and environmental context. We develop a covariance-aware Solar Gravitational Lens (SGL) framework for regional biosignature inference from reconstructed Einstein-ring measurements. A controlled 0.45-2.40 um Stokes-$I$ experiment uses ten illuminated cells, 128 channels, and R=70 to compare resolved and exactly projected disk spectra with common parameters and priors. Across 96 synthetic scenes, the joint gas, vegetation, and mineral block gains (1.52+/-0.03) nats after marginalizing cloud and calibration/response parameters; adding independently trained surrogate-discrepancy covariance gives (1.49+/-0.03) nats. Held-out mismatch nevertheless produces linearized shifts up to 6.08 posterior standard deviations; preserved precision does not establish unbiased recovery or evidence for life. For fixed Gaussian hypotheses, the expected log-likelihood-ratio loss under disk integration equals half the squared whitened contrast discarded by the projection. A separate 0.40-20 um continuum calculation provides absolute photon rates and observing-time estimates for an Earth-radius planet at 30 pc, observed from 650 AU. It includes source-averaged SGL amplification, finite-aperture extraction, coronal and host-star photons, detector noise, and a declared calibration floor. A reconstruction-covariance bracket reduces an 8 x 8 coadd gain from 7.77 to 3.00, costing 6.7 times the exposure in the statistical-noise limit. The framework connects regional spectroscopy and co-location tests to the physical and instrumental validation needed to assess exoplanet biospheres and possible biological activity.

♻ ☆ Bulk Phase Shift and Singularity
Yueke Jia, Manuela Kulaxizi
High-energy scattering of a light particle off a black hole at fixed impact parameter is described by an eikonal phase, which encodes the resulting time delay and angular deflection. This bulk phase shift admits a holographic interpretation as of the thermal momentum-space two-point function of a scalar operator in the CFT in the Regge limit. At small impact parameter, the phase shift acquires an imaginary part signaling inelastic scattering, obscuring the interpretation of time delay and deflection which become complex-valued. However, in a holographic CFT these quantities can also be extracted from the so called bulk-cone singularities of the position space thermal correlator. Extending this analysis to small impact parameters, we find that the position-space correlator develops a singularity precisely when a null geodesic reflects off the black hole singularity and reaches the opposite boundary. This provides a more robust identification of bulk time delay and angular deflection through singularities of position-space correlators.

This provides a straightforward way to isolate mergers originating from metal-poor environments. The determination of $z_t$ relies on the reconstruction of the cosmic star formation rate density as a function of iron abundance. This reconstruction is not unique, as it depends on the combination of different empirical scaling relations. Consequently, $z_t$ spans a broad range, from $z_t \sim 4$ to $z_t > 10$, depending on the adopted model variation. We present a statistical framework that enables rapid tests of astrophysical predictions against forecasted observations from next-generation \acrlong{gw} detectors. By quantifying variations in the binary black-hole merger-rate density between the target redshift and the local Universe, our approach maps evolutionary trends across parameter space and estimates the detection statistics required to distinguish genuine astrophysical variations from statistical fluctuations.

We investigate the late-time cosmological dynamics of a spatially flat FLRW Universe in the framework of exponential $f(Q)$ gravity, where $Q$ denotes the nonmetricity scalar. We present what are, to our knowledge, the first three-dimensional numerical-relativity evolutions of wormhole binaries: pairs of massive Ellis-Bronnikov wormholes held open by a phantom scalar field, whose energy density is nowhere positive. We construct constraint-satisfying initial data for single throats and for pairs, at rest and with orbital momentum, and evolve them with adaptive mesh refinement. An isolated throat is unstable: depending on the sign of a small perturbation, it collapses to a black hole or inflates, at the rate that linear perturbation theory predicts to within 1.9%. Two throats at rest repel when their scalar charges have the same sign and attract when the signs are opposite, with a strength ratio close to the scalar force law's prediction, so only opposite-signed pairs merge. A head-on collision forms a common horizon around both throats while they are still open. The horizon then loses 28% of its area as it absorbs the scalar field, and approaches the Schwarzschild radius of the pair's mass. Pairs that fly past each other form no horizon, and both throats inflate. Every encounter emits a short burst of gravitational waves and a scalar dipole wave of comparable, negative energy. An isolated collapsing throat rings at the quasinormal frequency of the black hole it becomes. No throat survives more than a few orbital periods, even when its initial perturbation is tiny, so these binaries do not inspiral. The results hold for one phantom-scalar model, equal masses, a single throat compactness and no spin.

These generalizations of the Bekenstein-Hawking entropy encode quantum gravitational, nonextensive, or fractal spacetime effects and can alter the gravitational entropy-area relation. In this paper, we demonstrate that the entropic force framework, when applied to galactic rotation curves and the baryonic mass of galaxy clusters, uniquely selects Tsallis entropy as the specific generalized entropy formulation. We then extend this Tsallis modified gravity to globular clusters to complete the structural hierarchy from galaxies to galaxy clusters to globular clusters and to investigate its behavior as a function of system scale. We will show that the nonextensive parameter exhibits no correlation with any of the macroscopic quantities characterizing gravitational systems, such as mass, radius, temperature, or density. Furthermore, it has previously been shown that entropy is not well-defined within the standard thermodynamic approach to gravity. The adoption of nonextensive statistics provides a foundation for entanglement, thereby enabling a consistent definition of entanglement entropy. We predict the existence of galaxy clusters with $δ= 1$ (i.e., clusters whose dynamics require no dark matter) analogous to $δ= 1$ systems already observed at galactic and globular cluster scales. This prediction provides a unique observational test to discriminate Tsallis gravity from $Λ$CDM and MOND. Therefore, for the entropic gravity paradigm to be consistent with observational data across all scales-from globular clusters to galaxies to galaxy clusters-it is inevitably required to be built upon \textit{Tsallis} entropy.

We show that another significant correction to the spectrum arises if the black hole is assumed to live in a thermal bath and the emitted radiation gets thermalised at the bath temperature. We argue that this altered decay rate has significance for cosmology and, in a realistic setting, show that it alters the life time of primordial black holes (PBHs) in the early universe. In particular, the very light PBHs formed right after the end of inflation decay faster which may have interesting phenomenological implications.

The usual path quantises the gravitational field in order to introduce the statistical structure characteristic of quantum mechanics. The procedure followed here instead is to remove the probabilistic element of quantum theory by using the less-common technique of introducing final boundary conditions as well as initial on the source. The relevant quantum formalism then becomes compatible with the non-statistical nature of general relativity and a viable theory can be constructed without difficulty. The view taken here is that the lack of both experimental guidance and theoretical consensus lends justification to considering such less mainstream ideas.

A scaling argument rules out any static vortex in the transverse plane, and the instability acquires a simple geometric meaning that shortens the path traced in SU(2) by the holonomy of a growing loop, lowering the winding by two. Quantum computing has been proposed as one response to this bottleneck: an n-qubit system can represent $2^n$ states simultaneously, although practical speedups require efficient algorithms, data encoding, and measurement strategies rather than superposition alone. Reported applications include brain tumor classification and segmentation on MRI, pneumonia detection on chest radiographs, skin and breast lesion classification, CT and PET reconstruction, and ultrasound denoising. Nearly all published systems are hybrid quantum-classical pipelines evaluated on small, downsampled benchmark datasets or simulators, and clinical deployment is not yet feasible. Within the optical-Dirac framework, the anomalous pair-creation and pair-annihilation terms of a bosonic Bogoliubov Hamiltonian correspond to couplings between the positive- and negative-frequency sectors, whose coherence underlies the Zitterbewegung response. When the constitutive parameters vary in time, the resulting moving-frame connection generates dynamical interbranch coupling and positive--negative-frequency coherence. Under periodic modulation, this coupling becomes resonant near $Ω\simeq2ω_0$, leading to parametric amplification of the coherence and consequently to an enhanced Zitterbewegung motion.
☆ Single-step SU(3) Hahn Echo in a Qutrit Atom Interferometer

The Hahn echo is a well-known dynamical decoupling method that refocuses the dephasing due to energy inhomogeneities of a spin-1/2 ensemble and is widely used to extend phase coherence in quantum computers and sensors. Extensions of such techniques beyond the spin-1/2 have been reported, but have mainly used SU(2) gates, limiting their scalability. Here, we generalize the Hahn echo to qutrits using single-step SU(3) gates and extend the coherence time by more than an order of magnitude. The gates are generated through optimal control theory and implemented in an ultracold atomic ensemble in free fall. A quantum process tomography procedure benchmarks the gates and yields fidelities of ~ 93%, limited mainly by state preparation and measurement errors. Due to the geometry of the laser beams, the generalized Hahn echo also realizes a three-path Mach-Zehnder atomic interferometer with two independent interferometric phase differences. Our results therefore establish SU(3) control for dynamical decoupling of qutrits and multi-path atom interferometers, with the latter opening the possibility for vector force measurements and interferometric tests of the validity of Born's rule.

☆ Quantum Evolution Networks Learn Long-Time Coherent Dynamics in Driven Spin Registers

Predicting and controlling driven quantum systems requires access to dynamics across physical parameters, initial states, and evolution times. A reusable neural model must capture this dependence while preserving unitary structure and maintaining accuracy over long-time coherent evolution. Here we introduce Quantum Evolution Networks (QENs), which map physical parameters and time to complete propagators for periodically driven three-spin registers. Shared networks learn unitary one-period propagators and compatible within-period paths, enabling predictions through known periodic composition without query-specific numerical integration. For transverse driving, the fifth-percentile fidelity, minimized over input states and sampled times, is 0.9947 over 24 periods on 256 held-out configurations. A leading-order analysis of spectrally resolved endpoint residuals predicts multicycle process error more accurately than quadratic or spectrum-averaged estimates. Interventions at matched single-period infidelity produce orders-of-magnitude differences in multicycle infidelity, demonstrating the importance of residual orientation. Compatible component replacements identify how endpoint and within-period approximations limit reconstruction accuracy. These results establish a reusable neural representation of the studied propagator families and connect its learned residual structure to its observed long-time reliability.

☆ Photon-Number Discrimination from Increasing Time-of-Arrival Separation in Wide Superconducting Microstrip Single-Photon Detectors
Hsin-Yeh Wu, Shu-Xiao Liu, Boris Tuchming, Xavier-François Navick, Pu-Kai Wang, Yi-Ren Wu, Jia-Wern Chen, Marc Besançon, Jean-François Glicenstein, Pisin Chen, Yu-Jung Lu, Stathes Paganis

Two \SI{10}{\um}-long devices with widths of \SI{3.2}{\um} and \SI{6.4}{\um} are characterized under pulsed \SI{515}{nm} excitation. The TOA histograms are described by sums of exponentially modified Gaussian (EMG) components, with the wider device exhibiting components assigned to photon numbers up to \(n=8\). Adjacent TOA peaks become more distinguishable relative to their widths at higher photon number, in contrast to the compression of neighboring photon-number timing shifts observed in conventional narrow-wire SNSPDs. For the components assigned to \(n=7\) and \(n=8\), the FWHM-normalized peak separation is \(2.15\), and the fitted EMG distributions yield an equal-prior pairwise TOA-assignment fidelity of \(99.6\%\). The EMG exponential-tail parameter \(τ_n\) decreases strongly with photon number, while the Gaussian-location parameter \(μ_n\) continues to shift between neighboring components. A phenomenological model motivated by absorption-site-dependent vortex processes and collective current redistribution captures these timing trends. These results support wide SMSPDs as a platform for TOA-based photon-number discrimination at high photon number, relevant to multiphoton-state characterization and photonic quantum information processing. The same geometry also provides a setting to examine how the spatial distribution of photon absorption affects vortex-assisted detection.

☆ Trident: Efficient Load Verification for Yoked Surface Codes using a Three-Level Memory Hierarchy ASPLOS '27
Gunagya Singh Mamak, Suhas Vittal, Kabir Dubey, Kaitlin N. Smith, Moinuddin K. Qureshi
Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computers (FTQCs) commonly use the surface code to encode program qubits as error-corrected logical qubits. Unfortunately, the surface code has a poor encoding rate, so recent work has proposed Yoked Surface Codes (YSCs), which concatenate the surface code with a high-rate quantum code. The surface code qubits in YSCs are protected by the checks, or yokes, of the high-rate code. YSCs have 1D and 2D variants, which are $1.8\times$ and $4.5\times$ more efficient than the surface code, respectively. Modern FTQC architectures use a two-level hierarchy: surface codes perform logical operations (compute) while 2D YSCs store idle program qubits (memory). To load a qubit from memory, the FTQC first performs retrieval, which logically moves a program qubit from a 2D YSC into a surface code (8 cycles). However, retrieval is not fault-tolerant, so the FTQC must verify the load by measuring all the yokes of the 2D YSC (178 cycles). As verification dominates memory access latency, eliminating it can provide a speedup of $5.7\times$. Our goal is to reduce the verification overhead of 2D YSCs while retaining their storage efficiency. We exploit the fact that 1D YSCs, though less storage-efficient, incur negligible verification latency. We propose Trident, which expands the two-level hierarchy into a three-level hierarchy by adding a small intermediate level containing a 1D YSC (L1). If most loads hit L1 rather than L2 (2D YSC tier), it can significantly reduce verification overhead. We present two variants: Trident-D (demand-driven) and Trident-P (prefetch-driven), which achieve speedups of $2.8\times$ and $4.2\times$, respectively, while increasing the physical qubit cost of memory by only 4.9%.

☆ Quantum Cryptomania with Classical Communication without One-Way Functions
Mohammed Barhoush, Amit Behera
In classical cryptography, one-way functions are necessary for most of cryptography. In the quantum world, however, Kretschmer at {TQC'21} and subsequent works have demonstrated that quantum versions of various primitives in minicrypt, such as signatures and private-key encryption, do not require quantum-computable one-way functions (\textsf{qOWF}s). However, the question of the necessity of \textsf{qOWF}s for primitives in Cryptomania like public-key encryption with classical public keys and ciphertexts (\textsf{qPKE}) has remained open. We provide a comprehensive picture of the relationship between \textsf{qPKE} and \textsf{qOWF}. First, our main result is a black-box separation between \textsf{qOWF}s and \textsf{qPKE}. In particular, we show that relative to a unitary, real, and self-inverse oracle, there exists a \textsf{qPKE} scheme (with classical keys and ciphertexts), but \textsf{qOWF}s do not exist. Further, our oracles admit a point-function obfuscation construction, thus ruling out black-box construction of \textsf{qOWF} from point function obfuscations. On the positive side, we construct \textsf{qPKE} from quantum indistinguishability obfuscation for quantum circuits with classical obfuscated descriptions and efficiently verifiable one-way puzzles, which is known to be a potentially weaker assumption than \textsf{qOWF}s, due to an existing black-box separation. Our construction is the quantum analog of the classical construction of \textsf{PKE} from one-way functions and indistinguishability obfuscation in the quantum computation with classical communication (QCCC) setting.
☆ Kinetic competition controls loss-induced exceptional points of Hubbard pairs
Ho-Kin Tang, Xiaosen Yang
Two-body loss can bind two fermions in a Hubbard lattice, yet the binding threshold in the infinite lattice need not be an exceptional point (EP). At fixed total momentum $\mathbf{K}$, the hops of the two particles interfere into a relative-motion hopping along each lattice direction, which sets the kinetic energy of the relative motion. On a hypercubic lattice, the threshold $g_c=1/[πρ_2(0)]$ is an EP precisely when the maximum kinetic energy along one direction exceeds the sum of the transverse maxima. This dominance keeps every transverse-momentum scattering channel propagating near the band center, making the local pair Green function purely imaginary there. Two real-energy scattering zeros associated with coherent perfect absorption then coalesce at the threshold into a second-order EP of the analytically continued pair problem, where loss restores the parity-time symmetry of the pair's scattering solutions. Without a dominant direction, binding occurs without coalescence and without breaking of that symmetry. Total momentum can therefore select EP sectors even on isotropic lattices. More broadly, the kinetic structure of the two-particle continuum determines whether loss-induced binding and exceptional degeneracy coincide.

☆ Material criteria for angular-momentum transfer from twisted photons to photoelectrons
A. A. Shchepkin, D. V. Karlovets
We study the material requirements for transferring the total-angular-momentum (TAM) projection of a twisted photon to the orbital angular momentum (OAM) of a photoelectron emitted from an $n$-type semiconductor surface. Within a single-valley effective-mass model of surface photoemission, we calculate OAM-resolved spectra for GaAs, InSb, $\mathrm{InAs}_{0.34}\mathrm{Sb}_{0.66}$, and $\mathrm{Hg}_{0.76}\mathrm{Cd}_{0.24}\mathrm{Te}$ irradiated by twisted photons with Laguerre--Gaussian--like momentum profile. The OAM transfer is characterized by the mean electron OAM, its root-mean-squared width, and the fraction of electrons with OAM-projection equal to the photon TAM-projection. Efficient transfer requires the transverse momentum of the conduction electron to be much smaller than the transverse momentum width of the photon, which favors low temperatures, small conduction-band effective masses, and shallow donor levels. GaAs is less favorable within the present model because of its larger effective mass and deeper donor levels. We also discuss the demanding photon-wave packet parameters, possible extensions to Dirac and Weyl semimetals, and post-emission OAM selection. Although the generation of vortex electrons with a vanishing OAM uncertainty via photoemission seems challenging, we argue that it is still possible to generate single-electron vortex states with a finite OAM dispersion.

☆ Real-space construction and selection rules of center-of-mass momentum eigenstates in two-dimensional many-body lattices
Ling Lin, Yongguan Ke, Chaohong Lee
We present a comprehensive framework for the real-space construction of center-of-mass (c.m.) momentum eigenstates in two-dimensional (2D) quantum many-body systems. Unlike standard momentum-space approaches, our real-space formalism explicitly captures the non-uniformity of cyclic subspace dimensions, which are fundamentally governed by the spatial symmetries of the many-body configurations and particle statistics. We demonstrate that performing 2D real-space translations on multi-particle states naturally induces non-trivial translation phase factors associated with the characters of these stabilizer subgroups, leading to a renormalization of permissible momentum values. Notably, we identify an anomalous cross-dimensional momentum coupling in highly symmetric particle distributions, where the permissible momentum values in one direction are strictly constrained by those in the perpendicular direction. We emphasize the algorithmic necessity of this coupling, as neglecting it leads to missing or duplicated basis states in numerical implementations. Concrete examples are provided to demonstrate the practical implementation and physical consequences of this framework.

☆ Robustness of Quantum Correlations and Controlled Teleportation Fidelity under Noisy Channels
S. Archana, Aditi Das, Venkat Abhignan, R. Muthuganesan
In distributed quantum computing, quantum networks provide a potential infrastructure for long-range quantum information processing. Controlled quantum teleportation (CQT) is a key practically relevant protocol that can connect two parties on a network and enables a third party, the controller to allow or abort the secure teleportation of an arbitrary single-qubit state between the two parties. We investigate the robustness of a three-qubit GHZ resource under bit-flip, phase-flip, depolarizing, and amplitude-damping noise. Using the Kraus-operator formalism, we characterize the noisy resource through multipartite quantum discord, genuine multipartite concurrence (GMC), localizable entanglement (LE), and CQT fidelity. We also outline a proof-of-concept photonic implementation for preparing the three-qubit GHZ resource and realizing the CQT protocol, which could enable experimental investigation of the effects of noise. Our results show that bit-flip and amplitude-damping noise generally preserve useful mutipartite quantum correlations over broader noise parameter ranges. Interestingly, multipartite discord exhibits freezing under bit-flip noise over a finite parameter regime. Moreover, discord can persist beyond the sudden death of genuine multipartite entanglement, revealing the distinct robustness of nonclassical correlations. We further demonstrate that CQT fidelity which characterizes the performance of CQT can exceed the classical threshold even after GMC vanishes, while LE more closely reflects the operational usefulness of the noisy resource. These findings highlight the complementary roles of quantum correlations and entanglement in assessing the resilience of GHZ-based protocols.

☆ Asymptotic scars arising from the remnants of quantum phase transitions
Leonard Logarić, Shane Dooley, Tsuyoshi Okubo, Nobuyuki Yoshioka
Many-body localisation, Hilbert space fragmentation and quantum many-body scars (QMBS) are well-established mechanisms of ergodicity breaking in quantum systems. Recently, asymptotic quantum many-body scars (AQMBS), non-thermal states whose stability grows with system size, have been proposed theoretically and probed experimentally. Here, we show that AQMBS arise naturally as remnants of certain quantum phase transitions. For a broad class of frustration-free Hamiltonians, we prove that their gapless excitations survive deformation into a scarred Hamiltonian as states whose energy variance is bounded by the excitation gap. Consequently, the gapless excitations at a quantum critical point become AQMBS of the scarred Hamiltonian. Their fidelity relaxation time is then set by the critical scaling of the gap, determined by the dynamic critical exponent. Modelling the critical Fredkin and Motzkin chains and the two-dimensional PVBS model, we obtain AQMBS whose variances directly reflect the dynamic exponents of the underlying transitions. Where the gap of the Motzkin chain closes super-exponentially, we find exponentially stable AQMBS, for which we also observe numerical evidence of volume-law entanglement.

☆ Can Spontaneous Time-Translation Symmetry Breaking Be Quantized Without Explicit Branches?
Partha Nandi
Can classically branched dynamics associated with spontaneous time-translation-symmetry breaking be quantized without explicitly retaining the branches of the Hamiltonian? We investigate this question using a reduced phase space. formulation in which the Hamiltonian is single-valued, while the critical structure of the classical Legendre map is encoded in a singular, momentum-dependent symplectic geometry. Quantization of the reduced Poisson algebra yields a deformed position-momentum commutator whose singularities determine distinct regular momentum sectors. Using the positive measure induced by the reduced symplectic structure, we identify a bounded central sector and two unbounded outer sectors. In the central sector, states with vanishing mean momentum obey a nonzero lower bound on position uncertainty, subject to the operator-domain assumptions of the representation. We further identify a possible field-theoretic connection with k-essence, where nonlinear scalar-field kinetics can produce finite-velocity degeneracies of the Legendre map. The relationship between the resulting reduced quantum description and branch-matching quantization remains unresolved and requires a comparison of the corresponding Hilbert spaces and operator domains.

☆ Additive uncertainty relations via pseudospectral methods
Alexander Cerjan, Lara Ismert, Terry A. Loring
Given Hermitian observable $A$, the variance of $A$ is given by the difference of expectations $\langle A^2\rangle - \langle A\rangle^2$, where the expectation of an observable implicitly assumes a choice of state for the underlying system. As a sub-case of a general lower bound for the sum of variances for finitely many arbitrary elements in a $C^*$-algebra, we prove that the sum of the variances for $d$ observables $A_1, \dots , A_d$ is greater than some expression in the expectations $\langle i[A_j,A_k]\rangle$ for $j\neq k$ plus the square of the smallest singular value of the associated localizer. In special cases, this expression is just a root mean square average. Our technique also derives a general containment between the Clifford pseudospectra and quadratic pseudospectra for $d$ observables.

♻ ☆ Universal quantum coding
Jacopo Rizzo, Filippo Girardi, Ludovico Lami, Jens Eisert, Lorenzo Leone
Entanglement distillation from noisy bipartite states and reliable quantum communication over noisy channels are fundamental tasks in quantum information theory. Yet existing coding schemes typically require prior knowledge of the underlying state or channel, or assume independent or weakly correlated quantum information sources. Here, using Schur-Weyl duality, we establish a universal quantum error-correction principle that overcomes these limitations. We show that the irreducible permutation spaces arising from the local Schur-Weyl decomposition of multiple copies of an unknown bipartite mixed state form maximally entangled quantum code spaces whose error structure is governed entirely by representation theory. Correcting these symmetry-resolved errors yields protocols for entanglement distillation and quantum communication that achieve coherent-information rates with exponentially vanishing error and optimal second-order corrections, even in the case of almost i.i.d. resources. Our approach also provides sharp finite-copy guarantees that are worst-case optimal at every finite block length, including in the sample-efficient regime, where the number of copies scales only polynomially with the number of qubits. Together, these results establish Schur-Weyl duality as a general mechanism for universal, robust, and optimal quantum coding, unifying entanglement distillation, quantum error correction, and quantum communication within a common representation-theoretic framework.

♻ ☆ A General Composition Theorem for Approximate Degree
Samruddhi Pednekar, Supartha Podder
A longstanding open question in Boolean function complexity asks whether approximate degree composes multiplicatively under block composition. Although a general multiplicative upper bound is known, matching lower bounds have previously been established only for restricted classes of functions. We resolve this question for all total Boolean functions by proving the matching lower bound. Together with Sherstov's upper bound, our result shows that, for every pair of total Boolean functions $f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}$ and $g:\{0,1\}^m\to\{0,1\}$, \[ \widetilde{deg}(f\circ g) = Θ\!\left( \widetilde{deg}(f)\,\widetilde{deg}(g) \right), \] where $\widetilde{deg}$ denotes constant-error approximate degree. We also consider the analogous question for exact quantum query complexity and give a counterexample showing that multiplicative composition fails in this setting.

Speech emotion recognition (SER) remains fragile in real-world conditions because emotional cues are subtle, speaker-dependent, and easily confounded by recording variability, while high-performing deep models typically rely on large and carefully curated training sets. Quantum machine learning offers an alternative way to introduce nonlinear correlation modeling with compact modules, yet existing quantum SER studies remain limited, and the impact of circuit structure is not well understood. This paper presents HQTN-SER, a hybrid quantum-classical framework that investigates how quantum tensor network connectivity can support SER under small-qubit settings. HQTN-SER introduces (i) an MPS-inspired quantum tensor network module that enforces structured interactions to model correlations in speech representations with a small number of trainable parameters, and (ii) a fusion strategy that combines quantum measurement features with a learned classical latent embedding for end-to-end emotion classification. We evaluate HQTN-SER on three public benchmarks (RAVDESS, SAVEE, and MDER) under a unified preprocessing and training protocol. The proposed model achieves test accuracies of 80.09\% on RAVDESS, 78.12\% on SAVEE, and 73.51\% on MDER, with corresponding macro-F1 scores of 0.8012, 0.7826, and 0.7351, respectively. The model also exhibits stable convergence while using only three or four qubits, suggesting that MPS-inspired circuit structure can be an effective and hardware-aware design choice for quantum-assisted SER. These results provide a compact experimental baseline for studying structured quantum modules in affective computing.

♻ ☆ Efficient Ground-State Manifold Amplification for Rydberg Atom Arrays via Houdayer Cluster Updates
Andrew J. Ochoa, Martin J. A. Schuetz, Helmut G. Katzgraber
We demonstrate a hybrid quantum-classical approach for exploring ground-state manifolds of maximum independent set problems, in which quantum hardware supplies the initial solutions and an entirely classical post-processing algorithm expands them, increasing the solution diversity of quantum hardware measurements by up to several orders of magnitude. Quantum optimization devices, while capable of generating high-quality solutions, can suffer from fundamental sampling limitations. This is particularly problematic for applications that strongly depend on a large variety of uncorrelated optimal solutions. We apply the Houdayer cluster update algorithm to systematically expand quantum-generated solution sets through classical post-processing. We validate our approach on a test bed of 43 problem instances from QuEra's Aquila analog annealing device, achieving diversity amplification factors, defined as the increase in the number of distinct solutions at a given set size, of up to 11923x with a median of 24.3x across different problem scales and hardness parameters. Because exact ground-state degeneracies are known for these instances, the recovered fraction of the manifold can be measured rather than bounded: post-processing recovers a median of 21% of the ground-state manifold, and provably all of it for six instances. We also demonstrate that, in some cases, the classical post-processing can discover independent sets larger than those found by the quantum hardware, thus improving on solution quality and not just diversity. While the method is non-ergodic and cannot guarantee complete manifold coverage, it consistently discovers a larger number of high-quality, and in some cases strictly better, configurations than quantum sampling alone. This work demonstrates how simple classical post-processing can enhance the utility of quantum optimization results.

With a common NumPy executor, Heavy has the lowest combined planning and execution time among five configurations on the runs that all of them completed. ♻ ☆ Freezing and Shielding under Global Quenches for Long-Range Interacting Many-Body Systems
Daniel Arrufat-Vicente, Nicolò Defenu
We investigate how local perturbations spread on long-range interacting spin chains and show how their nonequilibrium behavior exactly matches the one of a Fermi-Hubbard model with long-range hoppings. We then focus on the thermalization of the fermionic model following a sudden quench of local interactions between two distinct fermionic species. For both models, the quasiparticle spectrum consists of gapped low-energy levels, while the high-energy ones accumulate at a single point. When the low-energy gaps are large enough, turning on the local interactions does not effectively mix high- and low-energy modes, resulting in a freezing of the dynamical evolution. In general, the states within the excited subspace are shielded from the long-range signatures of the model, which are responsible for the low-energy extended states, and the dynamics effectively look as if long-range couplings were absent. This shielding mechanism becomes evident in the presence of disorder. It is shown that shielding and freezing are a universal feature of long-range interacting systems, and their relation to the existence of quasistationary states is conjectured.

♻ ☆ The Role of Quantum in Hybrid Quantum-Classical Neural Networks: An Empirical Assessment
Dominik Freinberger, Philipp Moser
Quantum machine learning has emerged as a promising application domain for near-term quantum hardware, particularly through hybrid quantum-classical models that leverage both classical and quantum processing. Although numerous hybrid architectures have been proposed and demonstrated successfully on benchmark tasks, a significant open question remains regarding the specific contribution of quantum components to the overall performance of these models. In this work, we aim to shed light on the impact of quantum processing within hybrid quantum-classical neural network architectures through a rigorous statistical study under ideal, noise-free simulation. We systematically assess a selection of commonly used HQNN architectures on three binary medical classification tasks covering medical signal data as well as planar and volumetric images. In doing so, we examine the influence attributable to classical and quantum aspects such as encoding schemes, entanglement, and circuit size. Within this experimental setting, we find that in best-case scenarios, hybrid models show performance comparable to their classical counterparts. However, in most cases, performance metrics deteriorate when the investigated QNN components replace matched classical processing layers. Our multi-modal analysis provides empirical insights into the contributions of the tested quantum components and advocates for cautious claims and design choices for hybrid models in near-term applications.

Combinatorial optimization is a leading target for quantum algorithms, but finite-depth QAOA can suffer from strong diabatic errors when the interpolation Hamiltonian has small, or exponentially small, spectral gaps. We propose a Pauli-sparse counterdiabatic extension of linear-ramp QAOA based on the regularised adiabatic gauge potential \[ \bigl(\mathcal L_H^2+ηI\bigr)A_λ^{(η)} = -\mathrm{i}\mathcal L_H(\partial_λH), \qquad \mathcal L_H(X)=[H,X]. \] Instead of computing a dense AGP, we solve this equation approximately by an inexact conjugate-gradient method in Pauli coordinates, truncating the Pauli expansion during the iteration to obtain a gate-budget-aware set of implementable rotations. The selected support is then improved by a Galerkin refit and certified by an a posteriori residual bound. The regularization parameter \(η\) acts as an energy-resolution scale: it suppresses transitions below \(\sqrtη\) while retaining larger-gap transitions. Thus, the method can avoid resolving exponentially small splittings inside a low-energy solution manifold while reducing leakage away from it. Numerical experiments on Ferromagnetic Chain (FC) and perturbed FC--MaxCut/MarketSplit instances show that the resulting LR-CD-QAOA ansatz improves approximation ratios over the uncorrected linear ramp, especially in regimes where LR-QAOA remains far from the optimum. Overall, the proposed regularized LR-CD-QAOA framework substantially broadens the practical applicability of QAOA to QUBO optimization by improving its robustness across heterogeneous problem landscapes, including instances with near-degenerate low-energy structures and small spectral gaps.
♻ ☆ Eigenstate condensation in quantum systems with finite-dimensional Hilbert spaces
Christopher David White, Michael Winer, Noam Bernstein
Random quantum states drawn from the Haar ensemble with a constraint on the energy expectation value $E_{\mathrm{av}} = \langle ψ| H | ψ\rangle$ display \textit{eigenstate condensation}: for $E_{\mathrm{av}}$ below a critical value $E_c$, they develop macroscopic overlap with the ground state. We study eigenstate condensation in systems with finite-dimensional Hilbert spaces. These systems display three phases: a ground-state phase, in which energy-constrained random states have macroscopic overlap with the ground state; a high-temperature phase, in which they have exponentially small overlap with each energy eigenstate; and an anti-ground-state phase, in which they have macroscopic overlap with the most highly excited state. In local spin systems the ground-state and anti-ground-state phases approach the middle of the spectrum as $1/[\text{system size}]$, but -- because the condensation phase transitions have exponential, rather than polynomial, finite-size scaling -- the crossover becomes exponentially sharp in system size and the high-temperature phase is best understood as an extended phase.
comment: Accepted version
♻ ☆ Transmitter-device-independent quantum key distribution
Qiang Zeng, Abhishek Mishra, Haoyang Wang, Zhiliang Yuan
Transmitter-side device dependence is a longstanding yet implicit problem in quantum key distribution (QKD), in contrast to the thoroughly addressed measurement-side case. Quantum steering, which intrinsically distinguishes the roles of sender and receiver in entanglement certification, offers a natural route to lifting trust assumptions on the transmitter. Existing one-sided device-independent (1sDI) protocols that exploit quantum steering as the security resource typically operate in a tripartite architecture, whereas adapting them to a transmitter-receiver architecture can introduce a signaling loophole. Here we conceptually formalize the transmitter-device-independence on the basis of faithful quantum steering and propose a practical transmitter-device-independent (TDI) QKD protocol within the 1sDI trust model. The TDI scheme operationalizes the implicit no-signaling condition by enforcing a causal isolation between the input information and the transmitted quantum states, thereby eliminating the associated transmitter-side device vulnerabilities. In a proof-of-principle experiment, we validate the feasibility of the TDI protocol, achieving a key rate in the asymptotic limit of 410~bps over 27~km spool fiber. By delivering TDI security while retaining strong loss tolerance, our approach helps bridge the gap between security and practicality for real-world QKD deployments.
comment: Accepted version
♻ ☆ Correlation Harvesting by Unruh--DeWitt Detectors in a Cylindrical Cavity: Entanglement, Mutual Information, and Quantum Discord
Shagun Kaushal, Harkirat Singh Sahota
We study correlations between two Unruh--DeWitt detectors coupled to a massless scalar field confined inside a cylindrical cavity through entanglement negativity, mutual information and quantum discord measures. The entanglement negativity follows the free space behavior for small energy gaps and small separation, while it gets enhanced for large energy gap as the off-axis detector reach cavity boundary. The entanglement island, where negativity is nonzero, gets extended for large energy gaps as compared to free space and the detectors can get entangled for large separations when one of them is placed near cavity boundary. In contrast, quantum mutual information and quantum discord remain nonzero over a substantially broader parameter range, including regions in which the negativity has vanished. However, these correlations are suppressed inside the cavity as compared to the free space correlations. Therefore, boundary conditions can selectively reshape the structure of harvested correlations in quantum field theory.

♻ ☆ Open quantum spin chains with non-reciprocity: a theoretical approach based on the time-dependent generalized Gibbs ensemble
Alice Marché, Hironobu Yoshida, Alberto Nardin, Hosho Katsura, Leonardo Mazza
We study an open quantum spin chain with non-reciprocal dissipation using a theoretical approach known as time-dependent generalized Gibbs ensemble. In the regime of weak dissipation the system is fully characterized by its rapidity distribution and we derive a closed set of coupled differential equations governing their time evolution. We check the accuracy of this theory by benchmarking the results against numerical simulations. Using this framework we are able to compute both the magnetization density and current dynamics, identifying some relations between the two. The problem of the anomalous power-law exponents identified in a previous work is discussed. Our work constitutes a theoretical approach that is able to describe the physics of non-reciprocal open quantum spin chains beyond analyses based on non-interacting fermions.

♻ ☆ Interpreting Liouvillian Eigenmodes: Quantized Orbits in Dissipative Systems
Ashlin V Thomas, Felix Fritzsch, Masudul Haque, Shovan Dutta
In closed quantum dynamics, energy eigenstates represent physical excitations which, for systems with a classical limit, localize on quantized orbits in phase space. Such a picture is lacking in open systems: Liouvillians have distinct right and left eigenstates that decay with time and are difficult to interpret. We recover a physical correspondence by introducing a gauge-invariant quasiprobability measure combining right and left eigenstates that interprets a Liouvillian mode as a set of coherences, allowing one to visualize the modes as quasiprobability distributions in a ``doubled'' phase space. Using this measure we show that, remarkably, a damped oscillator retains its quantized ``orbits'' for a large class of linear and nonlinear loss, with measurable signatures. A thermal bath broadens these orbits, similar to energy levels, leading to a characteristic multistage relaxation. This provides an experimentally accessible open-system analog of the eigenstate-orbit correspondence underlying semiclassical quantization. For quadratic systems, our results yield dissipative analogs of invariant tori - a central concept in Hamiltonian systems.
comment: 5 pages, 4 figures + appendix
♻ ☆ Constructing Large and Structured Decoherence-Free Subspaces in Hybrid Quantum Systems
Catalin-Mihai Halati, Tony Jin, Roderich Moessner
We develop a framework to construct large decoherence-free subspaces with a nontrivial structure. The construction is based on hybrid quantum systems in which quantum matter is coupled to a dissipative bosonic mode. Dissipation imposes a global constraint on the matter by selecting the matter null states in the long-time limit. The decoherence-free subspaces spanned by matter null states can exhibit exotic quantum properties and emergent symmetries that do not characterize the full Liouvillian dynamics. We show how to construct many-body operators with physically interesting null states by employing representation theory of Lie algebras. This approach allows us to choose models based on their underlying algebraic structure. We consider explicitly the example of coupling a lossy optical cavity to the directed tunneling operator in one-dimension. In this case, the symmetries of the decoherence-free subspace originate in an $\mathfrak{sl}(2,\mathbb{C})$ algebra, leading to an exponentially large number of steady states. We characterize the null states for both fermionic and bosonic particles, employing analytical and numerical methods. The states exhibit several properties that underline their complex quantum nature: long-range kinetic correlations and volume-law entanglement. The nonreciprocal nature of the directed tunneling dynamics leads to the emergence in the many-body regime of a symmetry-constrained Liouvillian skin effect. The open light-matter system exhibits a strong symmetry stemming from spinless $η$-pairing algebras. We show how the nontrivial properties emerge in the dissipative dynamics from generic initial states, by performing the quantum evolution of the hybrid open system with time-dependent matrix product state. Our framework opens avenues for dissipatively engineering complex quantum correlations and harnessing nonreciprocity in a controlled manner.
comment: ArXiv abstract abridged, see full abstract in the manuscript
♻ ☆ Authentication in Security Proofs for Quantum Key Distribution
Devashish Tupkary, Shlok Nahar, Ernest Y. -Z. Tan
Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) protocols rely on authenticated classical communication. Typical QKD security proofs are carried out in an idealized setting where authentication is assumed to behave honestly: it never aborts, and all classical messages are delivered faithfully with their original timing preserved. Authenticated channels that can be constructed in practice have different properties. Most critically, such channels may abort asymmetrically, such that only the receiving party may detect an authentication failure while the sending party remains unaware. Furthermore, an adversary may delay, reorder, or block classical messages. This discrepancy means that existing security proofs under honest authentication do not directly establish security in the practical authentication setting. We address this gap using an existing security definition from the literature that permits asymmetric aborts while retaining secrecy of any key produced and agreement of the keys whenever both parties accept. Our main result is a reduction theorem showing that, under mild and easily satisfied protocol conditions, any QKD protocol proven secure under the honest authentication setting, for the standard security definition with symmetric aborts, remains secure under a practical authentication setting, for the weaker security definition that allows for asymmetric aborts. This result allows all existing QKD proofs to be retroactively lifted to the practical authentication setting (with asymmetric aborts) with a minor protocol tweak.
comment: Accepted for publication at IEEE Transactions in Information Theory. Fixed a gap in the earlier version, and fixed an assortment of typos
♻ ☆ Field-Modified Quantum Potentials from Tridiagonal Representations: Analytical Spectra and Galerkin Simulations
Tunde Joseph Osunmusanmi, Berihu Teklu
We develop an effective radial framework for analyzing new field-modified potential function of a charged spinless particle in collinear electric and magnetic fields. Using the weak- magnetic field approximation, we neglect the diamagnetic term and other angular projections under an explicit smallness condition $\ll ΔE$, where $E$ is the electric field, and the replacement of the angular factor by $C=\cosθ$ in the spherical coordinates. The resulting equation is therefore a field-aligned radial model whose validity is limited to angularly localized states. Within this setting, we apply the indirect mode (or search mode) of Tridiagonal representation approach in the Laguerre and Jacobi bases. In the Laguerre basis, the tridiagonal constraint generates linear-plus-inverse and linear-plus-quadratic radial potentials, and the coefficient recurrences are connected with Meixner--Pollaczek and Meixner polynomial type structures, therefore yielding the analytic spectra and expansion wavefunctions. In the Jacobi basis, the mapping of the radial half-line to a finite interval produces a singular confining effective potential and a three-term recurrence that is treated through a truncated generalized eigenvalue problem. The formulation provides analytically and numerically tractable benchmark models for field-modified potential functions, while keeping the assumptions, parameter restrictions, endpoint behavior, and convergence tests explicit. In the Laguerre basis the resultant spectra are obtained in closed form and are independent of the orientation and of the electric field, which enter through the shape of the effective central potential, whereas in the Jacobi basis the spectrum is obtained numerically from a new three-term recurrence; in all cases the magnetic field enters through a linear Zeeman shift.
comment: 23 pages, 11 figures, 1 table
♻ ☆ Recent Advances in Quantum Architecture Search
Haozhen Situ, Zhimin He, Lvzhou Li
Variational quantum algorithms (VQAs) constitute a prominent paradigm for exploring the capabilities of near-term quantum computers. As the effectiveness of VQAs depends heavily on the design of variational quantum circuits, Quantum Architecture Search (QAS) has emerged as a critical research area to automate the discovery of high-performing circuit structures. This paper reviews key advancements in current research on QAS, including its core concepts, representative methodologies, applications, and emerging trends. The content is structured to ensure broad accessibility for a diverse audience of researchers while preserving the core principles of complex methodologies. In addition, we discuss remaining challenges and suggest potential research directions to offer perspectives on future exploration in this rapidly evolving field.
♻ ☆ MERA: A Mid-Circuit-Measurement Error-Aware Compilation Framework for Quantum Circuits
Ming Zhong, Zhemin Zhang, Xiangyu Ren, Chenghong Zhu, Siyuan Niu, Zhiding Liang
Mid-circuit measurement (MCM) enables qubit reuse and dynamic control in quantum processors, underpinning resource-efficient algorithms and quantum error correction. However, MCM introduces non-negligible errors, including measurement-induced crosstalk, idling-qubit decoherence, and reset infidelity. Additionally, MCM error rates vary across qubits within the same processor, with some exhibiting substantially higher errors. Existing compilers, including Qiskit-compiler and QR-Map, ignore MCM error variations, leading to fidelity loss in circuits with frequent MCM operations. In this paper, we present MERA, an MCM-error-aware quantum compilation framework that integrates MCM error modeling into the layout, routing, and scheduling stages. We first use the lightweight profiling method to capture a per-qubit MCM error distribution that remains stable for over 24 hours. The distribution guides MERA in applying MCM-error-aware layout and routing, while MERA further incorporates context-aware dynamic decoupling to improve fidelity. In evaluation, MERA delivers 24.94% -- 80.48% average fidelity gains over the Qiskit-compiler (optimization level 3) across different groups in selected benchmarks without additional SWAP overhead. It also boosts the fidelity of QR-Map-generated circuits by 29.26% on average (up to 122.58%), demonstrating its effectiveness for circuits with frequent MCM operations.
comment: 9 pages, 9 figures. Accepted by the IEEE/ACM International Conference on Computer-Aided Design (ICCAD 2026)
♻ ☆ Quantum-aware Transformer model for state classification
Przemysław Sekuła, Michał Romaszewski, Przemysław Głomb, Michał Cholewa, Łukasz Pawela
Entanglement is a fundamental feature of quantum mechanics, playing a crucial role in quantum information processing. However, classifying entangled states, particularly in the mixed-state regime, remains a challenging problem, especially as system dimensions increase. In this work, we focus on bipartite quantum states and present a data-driven approach to entanglement classification using transformer-based neural networks. Our dataset consists of a diverse set of bipartite states, including pure separable states, Werner entangled states, general entangled states, and maximally entangled states. We pretrain the transformer in an unsupervised fashion by masking elements of vectorized Hermitian matrix representations of quantum states, allowing the model to learn structural properties of quantum density matrices. This approach enables the model to generalize entanglement characteristics across different classes of states. Once trained, our method achieves near-perfect classification accuracy, effectively distinguishing between separable and entangled states. Compared to previous Machine Learning, our method successfully adapts transformers for quantum state analysis, demonstrating their ability to systematically identify entanglement in bipartite systems. These results highlight the potential of modern machine learning techniques in automating entanglement detection and classification, bridging the gap between quantum information theory and artificial intelligence.

♻ ☆ A Counterexample to the Optimality Conjecture in Convex Quantum Channel Optimization
Jianting Yang
This paper presents a counterexample to the optimality conjecture for the trace distance based optimal state transformation problem proposed by Coutts et al. [Quantum 5, 448 (2021)]. The conjecture posits that for the trace distance based optimal state transformation problem, applying the sign function to the error matrix uniquely determines a dual certificate for every optimal solution. By constructing a counterexample in 2-dimensional Hilbert spaces, we disprove this conjecture.
♻ ☆ Proof of Shor's conjecture on the accessible information of quantum dichotomies
Michele Dall'Arno
The accessible information of any given quantum ensemble quantifies the maximum amount of Shannon information that can be extracted from the ensemble by any quantum measurement. Almost three decades ago, Shor conjectured that the accessible information of any quantum dichotomy, that is, an ensemble of two states, is attained by a projective measurement. Recently, a proof of this conjecture restricted to the qubit case was published by Keil. Here, we conclusively settle this longstanding open problem. First, we show that Shor's conjecture follows, in arbitrary dimension, from a recent result by Fang, Fawzi and Fawzi, and we provide a self-contained, elementary proof. Second, for any given dichotomy and measurement, we provide the explicit construction of a projective measurement that outperforms such a measurement in extracting information from the given dichotomy. Third, while the computation of the accessible information is known to be non-convex in general, we frame the computation of the accessible information of dihotomies as a convex problem.

♻ ☆ Geometry-controlled zeros of resonant Kelvin-wave conversion in four spatial dimensions
Wei-can Yang, Xiang-dong Xu, Cheng Li, Ke-yu Lu
Geometry can suppress leading Kelvin-wave conversion even at exact momentum and frequency resonance. We demonstrate this on a vortex surface in four spatial dimensions. Perpendicular incidence removes the complete local-area four-wave coupling, exposing the finite nonlocal interaction carried by the surrounding fluid. Reflection keeps the quartets exactly resonant as their wave-number ratio varies. The flow restores conversion at generic ratios but develops a sign-changing zero of its own. Matching the complete Gross-Pitaevskii (GP) four-wave coupling establishes microscopic zeros whose ratios approach $λ_*\simeq 1.469$ at long wavelengths. Finite-domain GP calculations exhibit the sign reversal. Separate coherent-mixing and probe calculations relate the coupling sign to the generated-wave phase and the frequency ordering of reflection-even and reflection-odd modes. The result isolates a nonlinear effect of the surrounding flow and provides a phase-sensitive test of vortex dynamics beyond local tension.
comment: 37 pages, including Supplemental Material; 6 figures
♻ ☆ Dissipative dynamics and superradiant countinuous time crystal in a Rydberg-interacting Dicke system
Haohang Zhou, Xianfeng Chen, Luqi Yuan
The interplay between many-body interactions and controlled dissipation provides a rich setting for nonequilibrium quantum phases. We explore the superradiant phase transitions in a Rydberg-interacting open Dicke model with cavity loss and local dissipation. We find that the nonlinear feedback from atomic interactions stabilizes the atomic collective excited state and induces resonant collective motion, which can be further converted into robust superradiant oscillations with the inclusion of local dissipation. Beyond the mean-field approximation, we prove this system can support the finite-size local dissipative temporal order, i.e., continuous time crystal, from evidences of the decreasing damping of a finite-frequency Liouvillian mode and the linear-size scaling of quantum fluctuations. The correlation between the atomic colletive dynamics and the cavity photon number makes our findings easy to detect from output optical signal. By bridging interacting atomic matter and driven-dissipative cavity QED, our Rydberg-interacting Dicke model provides a unique spin-1/2 platform for exploring dynamical phase transitions and macroscopic temporal order in open quantum matter.
♻ ☆ Optimal Universal Bounds for Quantum Divergences
Gilad Gour
We identify a universal structural principle underlying the smoothing of classical divergences: the optimizer of the smoothing problem is a clipped probability vector, independently of the specific divergence. This yields a divergence-independent characterization of all smoothed classical divergences and reveals a common geometric structure behind seemingly different quantities. Building on this structural insight, we derive optimal universal bounds for smoothed quantum divergences, including quantum Rényi divergences of arbitrary order and the hypothesis-testing divergence. Our inequalities relate divergences of different orders through bounds of the form $D_β^{\varepsilon} \le D_α+ \mathrm{correction}$ and $D_β^{\varepsilon} \ge D_α+ \mathrm{correction}$, and we prove that the correction terms are optimal among all universal, state-independent inequalities of this type. Consequently, our results strictly improve previously known bounds whenever those were suboptimal, and in cases where earlier bounds coincide with ours, our analysis establishes their optimality. In particular, we obtain optimal universal bounds for the hypothesis-testing divergence.

♻ ☆ Coarse-Graining and Long-Range Response in Generated Systems
Jinku Guo
We study when a reduced description preserves the response to an applied source. For systems defined by continuously differentiable state updates and observations a bounded surjective linear coarse map gives differentiable descent when the projected maps are constant on each fibre. Their common source response is then preserved on the invertible domain. For approximate descent an exact error identity separates defects in the update and source coupling from defects in the readout and direct term. Resolvent and contour estimates carry these errors and the displacement of the reference branch to visible poles and their residues at shifted critical roots. In a reciprocal Hilbert-space realisation an isolated finite-dimensional critical subspace with a positive crossing matrix has a positive-semidefinite finite-rank residue when the endpoint operator is self-adjoint and the complementary inverse is bounded. Source overlap determines its visible directions. Arithmetic and reflecting-heat examples separate stationary response preservation from memoryless dynamical closure. In the two-mode example pole displacement decays geometrically with the retained memory length. The residue error includes an additional factor of that length. For a matched vacuum covariance the residue is the zero-mass atom of its positive spectral measure. This identification uses the same physical projection and source pairing together with the continuation and subtraction conventions and endpoint matching.

♻ ☆ Optimal phase estimation in the presence of correlated dephasing
Srijon Ghosh, Arkadiusz Kobus, Stanisław Kurdziałek, Rafał Demkowicz-Dobrzański
We investigate optimal metrological protocols for phase estimation in the presence of correlated dephasing noise, including spin-squeezed state sensing strategies as well as parallel and adaptive protocols optimized using tensor-network-based numerical methods. The results are benchmarked against fundamental bounds obtained either via the latest quantum comb extension method or an optimized classical simulation method. We find that the spin-squeezed states offer practically optimal performance in the regime where phase fluctuations are positively correlated but can be outperformed by tensor-network-optimized strategies for negatively correlated fluctuations.

♻ ☆ Succession of Ising criticality and its threshold in critical quantum Ising model subject to $X+ZZ$ decoherence
Yoshihito Kuno, Takahiro Orito, Ikuo Ichinose
We investigate a mixed state quantum criticality in the Ising model under $X+ZZ$ decoherence. In the doubled Hilbert space formalism, the decohered state resides on the self-dual critical line of the quantum Ashkin-Teller (qAT) model, as a result of the specific choice of the decoherence channel. On the other hand, since the mixed state under $X+ZZ$ decoherence satisfies the Kramers-Wannier self-duality in a weak sense, the Ising criticality of the pure state can be partially preserved in the mixed system. By making use of the combination of the doubled Hilbert space formalism and matrix product states, a numerical study is carried out. We numerically find that, up to moderate decoherence strength, the behavior of the mixed states on the critical line is consistent with Ising-like scaling within the accessible system sizes, with the effective central charge and critical exponents close to the Ising-CFT values $c=1/2$, $η=1/4$, and $η_X=2$. Our results of the central charge and critical exponents contradict the ones in the $c=1$ orbifold boson CFT describing the critical state of the qAT model. In addition, we also numerically observe the flow of the central charge up to strong decoherence. The strong decoherence washes out the remnant Ising criticality and induces strong-to-weak spontaneous symmetry breaking.

♻ ☆ Coupling phase interference effects in a multimode cavity magnonics system
M. Avicena, G. Bourcin, V. Vlaminck, J. Bourhill, V. Castel
Coupling phases play a decisive yet often overlooked role in cavity magnonics, particularly in complex multimode systems. Here, we investigate phase-mediated interference effects in a cavity magnonics system comprising a four-post re-entrant microwave cavity coupled to Yttrium Iron Garnet (YIG) spheres. Using an input-output model that explicitly accounts for both internal and external coupling phases, we achieve agreement with experimental microwave transmission measurements. Our results unravel the emergence of a positionally-dependent uncoupled mode due to interference of cavity photon-magnon (internal) coupling phases. Further, we experimentally observed large nonreciprocity at the antiresonance frequencies and show that this feature arises due to the far-detuned modes' odd parity cavity photon-probe (external) coupling phase interfering with the internal coupling phases. Bridging theory, simulation and experiment, these results establish coupling-phase engineering as a key principle for accurately modeling and designing multimode cavity magnonics devices.

♻ ☆ Resolving Nonlocal State Reduction via Induced Coherence in Frequency-Comb Biphoton Sources
Tai Hyun Yoon
How macroscopic definite outcomes and nonlocal correlations emerge from entangled superpositions across spacelike-separated regions without superluminal action or {\it ad hoc} wavefunction collapse remains a defining open question in the foundations of quantum mechanics. Here, we resolve this century-long paradox within \textit{linear} relativistic quantum electrodynamics by developing an open-system and measurement-defined framework realized in dual, spacelike-separated nonlinear crystals driven synchronously by a multi-mode optical frequency comb and seeded by an ultra-narrow coherent laser. Expanding the transverse electromagnetic vector potential into discrete single-photon frequency-comb supermodes, we show that tracing out the unmeasured continuous-wave idler field yields an exact spatial dephasing Lindblad master equation whose decoherence rate is governed by the non-orthogonal state overlap of single-photon-added coherent states. Connecting this open-system map to free-vector-space quotient measurement theory, we demonstrate that single-particle interference arises from the geometric projection of the composite state onto detector-defined conditional cosets rather than remote collapse, establishing strict operational equivalence across pump, seed, and signal phase scans. The resulting wave-particle-entanglement triality equality $P^2 + E^2 + V^2 = 1$ is saturated across the complete parameter space, while the atomic-clock-referenced comb structure anchors continuous-variable time-frequency displacement stabilizers directly at the hardware layer. Our work unifies induced coherence, Bohr's complementarity, and quotient measurement theory, providing a microscopic pathway toward fault-tolerant bosonic quantum information processing.

♻ ☆ Optimal Average Success Probabilities of Binary $(n,n-1)$ and $(n,n-2)$ Quantum Random Access Codes
Shuo Tan, Syed A. Jafar
A binary $(n,m)$ quantum random access code (QRAC) compresses an $n$-bit classical string into an $m$-qubit quantum state, from which a decoder attempts to recover a randomly selected target bit. Of particular interest is the optimal average probability of success, $P^{Q,\mathrm{avg},\mathrm{opt}}_{n,m}$, which was numerically conjectured to satisfy the bound $P^{Q,\mathrm{avg},\mathrm{opt}}_{n,m}\leq \frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{\frac{m}{n}}$. Recent constructions of $(n,n-1)$ QRACs by Suzuki and $(n,n-2)$ QRACs by Akibue et al. meet this bound exactly, raising the question of their strict optimality. In this work, we settle this question by proving the conjectured upper bound for $m\in\{n-1,n-2\}$, thereby precisely determining $P^{Q,\mathrm{avg},\mathrm{opt}}_{n,n-1}$ and $P^{Q,\mathrm{avg},\mathrm{opt}}_{n,n-2}$. The proof utilizes a translation recently studied by Lin and de Wolf from local to global reconstruction via pretty good measurement, along with dimensional and positive-semidefinite constraints on an induced channel.
♻ ☆ Lean-QuantumAlg: A Framework for AI Agents to Produce Quantum Algorithms that Humans Can Trust
Lei Zhang, Mingrui Jing, Yusheng Zhao, Jiahong Liu, Xin Wang
AI agents are increasingly capable of constructing quantum algorithms and proofs, yet machine-checked proofs alone cannot guarantee that the intended problem is solved or that resource claims match the verified computation. Here we introduce Lean-QuantumAlg, a Lean 4 framework for trustworthy AI-assisted development of quantum algorithms. Its Algorithm-Solves-Problem contract binds correctness, success probability, borrowed-state restoration and quantum and classical resource bounds to a single execution, while separating the guarantees that Lean checks from the problem specifications and execution models that humans review. We demonstrate the framework on nine AI-formalized quantum algorithms, from Grover search to quantum attacks on RSA-2048 and P-256, with less than 1% of each algorithm's imported source code requiring statement-level human review once the shared framework has been audited. By integrating reusable mathematical foundations, certified algorithmic primitives and execution-grounded verification, Lean-QuantumAlg provides a basis for AI agents to construct and certify quantum algorithms, opening a path toward scalable AI-driven discovery of quantum algorithms.

♻ ☆ Continuous-time evolution via probabilistic angle interpolation and its applications
Tomoya Hayata, Yuta Kikuchi
We explore the applicability of a stochastic time-evolution algorithm based on probabilistic angle interpolation. To simplify the pre-processing of the algorithm, we take the continuous-time limit, thereby explicitly eliminating Trotter errors and streamlining the resource analysis. We also introduce a noise-mitigation method tailored to it. ♻ ☆ Quantum Spectral Estimation with Multiple Initial States: Improved Error and Cost Scaling
Lingwei Zhang, Zhiyan Ding
We study quantum spectrum and eigenstate property estimation using multiple initial states and generalized Hadamard tests. Building on the QFAMES (quantum filtering and analysis of multiplicities in eigenvalue spectra) framework, we introduce a new method that samples evolution times independently for each initial-state pair. Under the stated assumptions, when statistical error determines the sampling cost, the total Hamiltonian simulation cost required for fixed-accuracy eigenvalue and observable estimation is independent of the number of initial states, up to logarithmic factors. This improves scalability when many initial states are needed to explore the target eigenspaces. The method also reduces the cost of multiplicity recovery and retains Heisenberg-limited scaling for eigenvalue estimation. Numerical experiments support the predicted statistical error scalings.

☆ All-multiplicity $\textrm{AdS}_4$ correlators in the self-dual sector
Humberto Gomez, Renann Lipinski Jusinskas, Arthur Lipstein, Cristhiam Lopez-Arcos
It was recently shown that tree-level gluon correlators of any multiplicity in $\textrm{AdS}_4$ admit an expansion in terms of flat-space scattering amplitudes, where lower-point amplitudes in the expansion depend on merged external data. We derive here analogous formulae for correlators of scalar theories which encode the self-dual sectors of Yang-Mills theory and gravity in this background. In the latter case, the amplitudes are differential operators which can be obtained from the former using a simple double copy prescription in terms of kinematic numerators satisfying color-kinematics duality.

☆ All Order Self-Dual Correlators From Symmetries
Chandramouli Chowdhury, Silvia Nagy
We consider the scalar actions for self-dual Yang-Mills and self-dual gravity. We give a novel resummed version of their infinite tower of symmetries. We show that the Ward identities for symmetries corresponding to the individual levels of the infinite tower give the soft limits for wavefunction coefficients, while their resummed version completely fixes the full wavefunction. Our analysis is valid for general boundary conditions. Finally, we give an explicit formula for the $n$-point wavefunction coefficient as a single determinant reorganising the perturbiner solution, which also satisfies the soft limits.
